maintopic: CANNED AND SALTED-DISCONTINUANCE OF INTERNATIONAL ALLOCATION

speakeroldname: Hon. H. F. G. BRIDGES (Minister of Fisheries):
maintopic: CANNED AND SALTED-DISCONTINUANCE OF INTERNATIONAL ALLOCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce that after March 31. 1947, no Canadian canned fish will be subject to international allocation. Similarly, allocation of salted cod and other salted groundfish of 1946 production will come to an end on June 30 of this year, and there will be no allocation of salted fish from 1947 production. Examination of the world situation by the international food emergency council at Washington this week has shown the world supply is coming into approximate balance with effective demand, when all fish products are taken into consideration; hence this decision has been made to discontinue the allocation schemes relating to canned and salted fish.
Most Canadian canned fish has been subject to international allocation since the mid-war years. Chief among the products concerned have been canned salmon and canned herring, but the list has also included such others as canned sardines, mackerel, groundfish and pilchards. All of them will come out from under this control at the close of the present month.

That settles it-the 2nd until the 8th. I am not putting this on any personal basis, because if there is anything one dislikes it is discussions in the House of Commons which are sectional. I put it on the ground that we can do the country's business much better with a short adjournment than we can with a long time. I am sure hon. members will agree that last year after we left here the casualties among people who were simply worn out were greater than any of us knew, if a census could have been taken. There is a further reason. We have here a hard-working civil service and many of them are quite unable to get away for a natural and proper holiday until the house adjourns. Vacation time for these people is in the months of July and August. Last year they were unable to have any proper holiday at the proper time. I may add one other section of our people, the press gallery. They must stay here as long as we do.
I have been told by senior members that it does not matter how long vacations are, the session will be just as long. I do not agree with them, but if they are right it is a sad commentary on our way of doing business, and there should be a change.
I suppose the financial aspect of it is neither here nor there, but I am quite sure that many of us will come back fully revived after a week's vacation. We shall have been sitting for only two months when we leave here on the second. I am asking the consideration of the house for my suggestion; in fact I am inviting hon. members to vote against the resolution, knowing, as the Prime Minister assured us, that there are two alternatives, and that the other would then be adopted.

Mr. Speaker, if I were moving an amendment to this motion, I would move one entirely different from the suggestion of the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith). It is a well-known fact that of all the members of parliament none make greater sacrifices with respect to business and family life than the members from the far-off Pacific coast. They are here sometimes as long as six and a half or seven months. If I had my way I would move for an adjournment of a weekend, or for the period from Thursday until Tuesday. If any hon. members think that those from distant places like to sit around
Ottawa until members from Ontario and Quebec return, they had better give a little more consideration to members from British Columbia coming back on the fourteenth. I ask the hon. member for Calgary West to consider those of us who come from the Pacific coast. The time he is suggesting will not be sufficient to enable us to go home.

Mr. Speaker,
it is not very often that I differ from my good friend the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith). I am not yet one of those who have become full-time parliamentarians, and I think there are many others like me. I agree with the hon. member who has just taken his seat. I suggest that these recesses be arranged so that members from great distances may do their travelling over the week-ends. That is an important point to those who come from a distance. Many hon. members in the east are privileged to be able to go home on week-ends and look after their businesses. Recently special arrangements have been made to get them home on week-ends so that they can stay here the full week.
I am very serious about this. I think we should have at least a reasonable recess for Easter so that those who are farmers or business people can go home. Farms or business undertakings do not just run themselves throughout the year without some little supervision at times. In the last parliament the Prime Minister spoke about the difficulty of getting candidates for this House of Commons. If persons who retain an interest in business of one kind or another are to run for parliament they must be given some consideration so that they can look after their businesses or farms as well as attend to the business of the country here. Over the last seven years since I have been a member of the house we have been spending the greater part of the year in Ottawa. In arranging these recesses in the future, consideration should be given to the matters I have mentioned, with particular reference to members who live a long way from the capital. Another suggestion I might make is this. In view of the transportation arrangements which have been made for members from the two great central provinces, consideration might be given to those who come from great distances, both east and west, to the extent of permitting travel by air every so often throughout the year.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister said yesterday that his desire was to have the adjournment to suit the convenience of the general member-
Easter Recess

ship of the house. I am sure he meant that. The adjournment which is proposed, from Wednesday, April 2, until Monday, April 14, is an adjournment of eleven days. That is not a long enough time to allow those who live a long distance from Ottawa to make the trip home, spend any time there and come back. They would be travelling most of the time. I think all members will agree that it is the desire to get through the business of the session as early as possible. I suggest, with all due respect to the Prime Minister, that the adjournment begin on Thursday, April 3, and extend until Tuesday, April 8. That would be five days. No one who has to stay in a boarding house or hotel wants to spend a long adjournment in Ottawa at this season of the year, when the ground is covered with several feet of snow. There is nothing attractive about it. I suggest that five days is ample.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE ON ACCOUNTS AND ESTIMATES OF GOVERNMENT OWNED TRANSPORTATION LINES
speechtext:
I should like to ask the minister one or two questions about the functions of this committee. When it was first appointed, about fifteen years ago, the understanding was that it would make an examination along certain lines, not only of accounts but of matters of policy. It is contended that the committee of supply loses all its functions through the appointment of this committee. How many meetings did the committee hold last year? Very few. They sat around a table and discussed certain features, but forgot all about improvements to
[Mr. G. Black.1

Railways and Shipping
the system. They discussed the spending of money on subsidiaries in the United States, while the Canadian service was neglected. It seems to me that in connection with the Canadian National Railways, charity begins at home. Is this the best system we can devise for administering a property worth hundreds of millions of dollars, and ocean services, hotel services, and last but not least the work of Trans-Canada Air Lines? As far as I know the members of this committee have very little knowledge of transportation or financial matters; and through the appointment of this committee we are losing the whole jurisdiction of parliament over the administration and financing of this great corporation, which gave such splendid service in Canada and on the oceans all during war.
Last year this committee forgot one important matter, that is, the work done during the war by' employees of the railway of all ranks. Some of the conductors and others engaged in handling the trains worked eighteen hours a day and the great success enjoyed by the Canadian National and our other transportation system all during the war, their efficiency and the safe manner in which they operated in all kinds of weather, handling the demobilization of troops and transporting them from the seaboard right across Canada, was due in no small part to the work of these men. It seems to me the committee forgot all about that last session, and about a war bonus for them, too.
I believe the time has come when some further examination of this system should be carried out. If it is a public ownership venture let us have real public ownership, not the brand we are getting at the present moment. They have moved their offices from the province of Ontario, where they make most of their money, to another place. The auditor general, I might add, has nothing to say about this system, though he does have something to do with some other public ownership ventures. Now we are removing this system from the control of the committee of supply; and. parliament, which came into being to exercise jurisdiction over the tax rate and the expenditure of money, has practically ceased to function in this regard. This system has its own auditors, who are changed practically only when the government changes. I have read the reports of these auditors, but have failed to find1 any improvements recommended in connection with this great public utility. I believe the time has come when the minister should give some explanation as to the functions of this committee, and what it does; what changes it has advocated, and whether
the minister thinks this is a proper policy. I believe some experts should be engaged to find out what is going on in that system. These committees do not know what is going on, but when their report is presented it will be too late the last day of the session for us to do anything but concur in it. It seems to me the committee of supply has ceased to function, and I believe a better policy should be recommended by the system itself to the minister.
Motion agreed to.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have not seen the letter said to have been written by General Eisenhower, and therefore I cannot tell what he said. Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved the third reading of Bill No. 23, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935.

Mr. Speaker, the house may find it a bit strange that I should want to take part in this debate. But if I do, it is first of all to approve the principle of the bill as set out, and secondly because I am keenly interested in the method of transportation of wheat and other grains.
Since the bill has been under discussion some criticism has been levelled at the government, with reference to the movement of grain and this criticism has been of such a nature that I believe a reply should be made at this stage. If in Canada there has been some difficulty with reference to the transportation of grain, it is, as the house knows, due particularly to the acute shortage of box cars. I believe hon. members will be interested in the position with reference to box cars generally, because the matter has been discussed in the press on more than one occasion, and again in the house.
The present box car situation in Canada is acute. Summing up as briefly as I can, I believe the situation can best be stated by saying that at this time there are some 117,000 box cars in Canada. Of that number 26,000 are in the United States, about 44,000 in western Canada and approximately 47,000 in eastern Canada. Of the 44,000 in western Canada about 11,000 are used for the transportation of grain, and the balance for other commodities. However, for the transportation of wheat and other grains there are required a far larger number than 11,000. In fact there are required some 8,000 or 9,000 more box cars for this purpose than is available at present in western Canada.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
The situation in eastern Canada is substantially the same. About 47,000 box cars are used for the transportation of various commodities, including feeds, from lake ports and bay ports to Atlantic seaboard ports. There is an acute shortage here, as well, of somewhere in the neighbourhood of 15,000.
To what extent is the shortage, arising from cars being in the United States, compensated by United States cars which are in Canada?

I was going to deal with that in a moment, but to answer the hon. member immediately-and of course I am speaking only from memory on the point- while I stated there were some 26,000 Canadian box cars in the United States, there are approximately 18.000 United States box cars in Canada. So that there is an adverse balance against Canada on this score of 8,000 box cars. This, however, is offset by the large number of hoppers and refrigerator cars which belong to United States companies, 'but which are in Canada.
I return now to the general position respecting the shortage of box cars. Why is there a .shortage? I have said that there is an acute shortage in eastern Canada, to the extent of some 15,000 cars. Dealing now more directly with wheat, let me say that early in January of this year an understanding was reached as to the number of box cars required for the wheat movement. Had it not been for the extreme weather conditions in western Canada I do not think the situation in that part of the country would have been as serious as it was for a time, and as perhaps it is now to some extent.
The position was fairly satisfactory until about the middle of January, when, because of storms in western Canada, it became more acute. At that juncture, in conjunction with the railways, the transport controller issued a priority order in favour of grain, and that order had the effect of diverting from eastern to western Canada some 2,400 to 3,000 box [DOT]cars. This procedure met with a large measure [DOT]of success in meeting the situation for the time being. Industries in eastern Canada, however, felt the shortage, and many of them pointed to the fact that unless something were done to give them assistance they might have to close their doors. After further consideration of the whole picture, again in conjunction with the railways, the transport controller decided to do away with the priority -order for grains, and the position today is that the matter is placed squarely on the ;shoulders of the railways.
Another reason for the shortage points to the coal strike in the United States. One effect of that strike was that most of the canalers used for the transportation of grain were commandeered during the navigation season for the purpose of transporting coal. Every one knows how serious the coal situation was at one time. Had it not been for the measures taken by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) and the coal control, which existed at that time, I do not think the position with reference to coal during the winter season 1946-47 would have been nearly as good as it was.
Over and above that the railways had the added burden of having to move grain as they normally do during the winter season. They had the additional task of transporting grain from the lakehead and the bay ports during the winter season. This added greatly to their problems and brought about a position which has led to some complaints. It has been stated in a certain editorial that grain is being diverted from Canadian to American ports. That is not so; it is not an accurate statement. Grain has not been diverted from any Canadian port to an American port. Grain has always been moved through American ports. For instance, in normal times grain moves through Baltimore, Philadelphia, Boston, Portland, Buffalo, and Erie. Canadian grain has always moved via the Erie canal and down the Hudson river. During 1946-47 the movement of Canadian grain through American ports has been fifty per cent lower than in any other season.
Some charges have been made with reference to the port of Saint John, and it has been said that grain was diverted from Saint John to Portland. I was aware of the editorial which appeared in a certain Saint John paper on March 8; it came to my attention on March 11.'I have read it carefully, and there are many inaccuracies in it. I should like to deal briefly with that for a moment in connection with the situation generally. There has never been a tie-up of ships in the port of Saint John because of a lack of grain. Take March 11, for instance, the day on which this editorial came to my attention. That is a typical day because the position on March 11 is the position which has obtained in that port during the whole season.
On March 11 there were 31 ships in the port of Saint John. Four ships were unloading; fourteen were loading other commodities; five were ready to take on grain; six were fitting and awaiting berths, and two were being repaired. Here is the position with reference to grain in that port on that particular day. There were 348.000 bushels loaded on two
Canadian Wheat Board Act

steamers, and as I say there were five ready to take on grain. There were 608,980 bushels in the elevators and there were 502,000 bushels loading in the three steamers at the berths. That left a favourable balance of wheat in the elevators of 96,980 bushels. Over and above that there were in transit east of Monk
1.200.000	bushels of wheat, making a total of 1,297,180 bushels. For the six steamers which were waiting berths, there were required
1.024.000	bushels, which left a favourable balance of wheat of 273,180 bushels in the port of Saint John.
It has been stated that at the very hour when wheat was being diverted from Canadian ports to American ports there were ships in the harbour of Saint John unable to get grain. May I reply to that by saying that at no time were there ships in the harbour of Saint John unable to get grain. On the contrary the ships there were ships unable to get berths because there was too much business. Business was so good at the port of Saint John that certain American companies, becoming tired of waiting for berths, transferred their ships to the port of Halifax.
The hon. member for St. John-Albert stated that the press report to which he referred was one week prior to March 11, which would be March 4. I do not see how the minister's remarks would apply.

I have not the details for March 4, but I am informed by the transport controller that conditions on that day were practically the same as on March 11. If the house will permit me I should like to deal with the port of Halifax, and I am sure the hon. member who has just interrupted me will be interested in the position there. On the same day, March 11, there were 110,000 bushels of grain in the elevators at Halifax, There were 82,000 bushels in box cars. This made a total of 192,000 bushels. There were required for the steamers in the port ready to load a total of 197,000 bushels. The house will note therefore a deficit of some 5,000 bushels, but there were in transit east of Monk a total of 204,000 bushels of wheat in some 120 box cars and west of Monk there were 174 box cars in transit carrying wheat to that port.
Is that the same wheat the minister referred to as being en route to Saint John?
Oh, no.
The minister said east of Monk.

One was via Canadian National and the other was via Canadian Pacific. I thank the hon. member for the correction. It follows that so far as the port of Halifax is concerned there was an ample supply of grain for incoming steamers.
May I interrupt the minister to ask one question? Were ships diverted to the port of Portland as the editorial states?

The editorial I have
before me refers to the diversion of ships from the port of Saint John, and from what my hon. friend has said I take it it refers to a diversion from the port of Halifax as well, although I do not recall reading that. Ships were not diverted from the port of Saint John or the port of Halifax to Portland. I repeat that grain moves normally to United States ports and ships were diverted from one American port to another. Instead of going via Buffalo or via Erie, it went via Portland. Why? Because the haul to Portland is much shorter. I am informed that the distance from Montreal to Portland is 295 miles and that it takes from twelve to sixteen hours for a box car movement to that port. The distance from Montreal to Saint John is 488 miles, and it takes three days for a box car movement to that port. The distance from Montreal to Halifax is 800 miles, and it takes four days for a box car movement to that port. The Canadian National Railways have a line operating directly from Montreal to Portland. When they make the movement to Portland they use their own box cars all the way. They can be earmarked so that they come back the next day, whereas if they go by other ports they may be lost and held up for some weeks.
As I said to the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) a moment ago, there are a large number of United States box cars in Canada, but there are a larger number of Canadian box cars in the United States owing to the fact that it is often almost impossible to earmark them once they get south of the border.
To the charge that workers were being deprived of work and wages because of this diversion, I say that is not so, because in the first place there has been no diversion from a Canadian port to a United States port. That is not so because the operation took place on the lines of the Canadian National Railways. Many of the workers who were employed on these lines are Canadians, and all of the profit and money derived therefrom enures to the general benefit of Canada.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
I should have said that the normal cycle for a box car is twelve days-that is, from the time it leaves its point of departure until it returns equals a period of twelve days. The average movement from Montreal to Portland is four days; therefore the saving so far as box cars themselves are concerned was a great one in that instance.
With reference to the movement of box cars generally the transport controller, in conjunction with the railways, has a most difficult task to perform. I can assure the house that because of the storms, because of the position which I outlined at the beginning of my remarks, it is difficult to satisfy all the requirements. There is grain from the country to Vancouver which must be moved; there is grain from the lakehead; there is feed from the lake and the bay ports down to Ontario and Quebec; there are other commodities such as pulpwood and newsprint which must be moved south of the border, and there are commodities of industries which require attention as well. My colleague points out to me that feed to the maritimes is also an important matter which I should not have overlooked.
Has the minister any information as to Pacific coast ports?

I am sorry, I have not. The editorial dealt only with the ports of Saint John and Halifax, but I shall be glad to get the Vancouver figures for my hon. friend.
I think the house will agree with me when I say that the railways have a most difficult task with reference to the movement of grain. I believe they have done a good job under all the circumstances. They feel that if all priorities are removed they will be in a better position to handle the grain than if there are priorities. I have figures for the movement of wheat in western Canada. I do not want to put these on Hansard because I have them not to March 13 but only to March 7. They indicate that there has been a movement all along the line from March 1 to March 7, on the average of 752 cars to 800 cars a day, which under all the circumstances is pretty fair. I therefore submit to the house that the railways have done a good job under the circumstances, and if the matter is left to them with the assistance of the transport controller, I think grain will move freely throughout the country.

Before the minister takes his seat, will he answer one question if he has the information? Can he give the house the relative amount of freight in the form of western grain which passes through the Canadian ports, say at Montreal, Saint John and Halifax, as compared with United States ports such as Portland, Boston, New York, and others? Has the minister those figures?
I am sorry; I have not that.

Will the minister permit one more question? Has he any record of the amount of demurrage which the British government had to pay or was charged on shipments of wheat, caused by the hold-up of ships at our ports in Canada during the past fall?

I would not have the information to reply to that question in any event, because the transport controller has nothing to do with demurrage. But my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) has drawn to my attention the fact that generally speaking we do not pay demurrage-at least the wheat board does not pay it.
That is not my question. I want to know how much the British government had to pay.
We have no information on that point.
A more important question is why they had to pay.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I am sure the house has listened with interest to the statement of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) as to the shortage of box cars and its effect on slowing up the shipment of grain. In my remarks at this time I do not propose to deal with that matter. I am rising to do two or three things. I wish to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce to answer certain questions which we asked in previous stages of the debate on this bill, and to ask certain other questions with respect to the negotiation of the prices to be paid on next year's crop, and before I sit down I propose to move an amendment, that this bill be not now read a third time but be referred to the committee of the whole to reconsider sections 20, 21 and 22 for the purpose of trying to have the government pay the participation payments on the 1945 crop.
At previous stages in the consideration of this bill certain questions were asked. I think I am correct in saying that these particular ones were not answered: First, how much of the farmers' money the government is holding on the 1943 crop, the 1944 crop and the 1945 crop. It is not so important about 1943; I imagine that is largely paid out by this time,
Canadian Wheat Board Act

I do not think the minister answered these questions when I asked them; he did not at that moment have the information available.
Then I asked the minister what was the average rate of interest to the government or the wheat board on these moneys which are being held back and not paid out to the farmers.
I want to know the balance in the government's hands for the 1945 crop particularly, because the crop of that year was sown and harvested and nearly all sold before the British wheat agreement was signed. The British wheat agreement was signed early in July of 1946 and applied to the four following years, 1946, 1947, 1948 and 1949 crops. When the government came to making the pooling arrangement they included with these four years the balances held for farmers on the 1945 crop. I do not know that the house fully appreciated that fact in earlier stages of the debate. The wheat agreement applied particularly to the crops of 1946, 1947, 1948 and 1949, but when the government came to make the pooling arrangement they said they would take in the balances due on the 1945 crop and add them to any balances in the other four years; then if there was any left at the end of 1950 they would pay it out at that time.
I want to know what these balances are, because, whatever certain growers or organizations may have had in mind with respect to the balances due on the 1916, 1947, 1948 and 1949 crops, it was never in their minds that any balance due on the 1945 crop should be included in that pooling arrangement. I want to know the amount held back for that year because the organized farmers desire to have that balance particularly paid back to them without waiting until the year 1950.
Hon. members will recall that in committee of the whole I moved that, instead of keeping all these balances until 1950 and paying out whatever may be left at the end of 1950, the balance should be paid each year. The committee did not accept that amendment. By a vote of 88 to 31. if I remember correctly, that amendment was turned down. I do not therefore intend to waste the time of the house by asking for further consideration of that particular proposal now. I expect that, since the government members and certain other sections of the house opposed it, it would be turned down again. But I wish to raise the question with regard to the payment of the balance for the 1945 participation certificates. In that connection I wish to read from the representations by the Canadian Federation of 
Agriculture in its presentation to the dominion cabinet on February 28 with respect to agricultural matters in general.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) read certain sections of that report in support of certain aspects of the bill before us, but I want to read what that organization, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, had to say with respect to this particular matter of the payment of the balance on the 1945 crop. This crop, as I said, was sown and harvested and nearly all sold before this agreement was entered into. This is what the federation had to say to the government in its presentation for this year:
. . . We protest the action of the government in not retiring participation certificates on wheat delivered to the Canadian wheat board during the crop year 1945-46. We cannot but regard the withholding of these payments as contrary to the understanding which wheat growers had with the government during the whole of that crop year. We strongly urge that any surplus on hand resulting from the operations of the crop year, 1945-46, be paid to producers now and not pooled with the operations of subsequent years.
That is (he one thing I urge particularly in asking that the government permit this measure to go back to the committee of the whole in order to reconsider the matter.
There are also some other questions which I wish to ask the minister. These have to do with the price to be paid under the British agreement for the 1948 crop, next year's crop. Under the British agreement, the British government undertakes to pay not less than $1.25 for next year's crop. But in that agreement there is also an undertaking that the actual price to be paid on next year's crop shall be negotiated before the end of December of this year. It is with respect to the attitude of the Canadian government on the price which will be set before this house meets again. It is the attitude of this government towards the price to be negotiated on that 1948 crop, that I wish now to direct some questions to the government.
In order to make clear my position let me read first of all section 2(a) of the British wheat agreement:
The actual prices to be paid for wheat to be bought and sold within the crop year 1948-49 shall be negotiated and settled between the United Kingdom government and the Canadian government not later than the 31st December, 1947.
It is clearly set out in a previous section of the agreement that the price shall not be less than $1.25. In this section it is set out that the actual price shall be negotiated before December 31 of this year. I think this

Canadian Wheat Board Act
house and the Canadian people should know something of the attitude of the government toward the price which the government will attempt to secure when they negotiate the matter some time before December 31.
I would like the government to answer these questions as specifically as they can. Does the government propose to sell the 1948 crop below the world price? That was done for this year's crop. We know something of what the world price is today. We know what the quotations are for September next, though we do not know what they will be in December. The September price quoted now in Chicago is $2.25 per bushel. Does this government propose to sell the 1948 crop below the world price as it did the present crop? If so, how much below the present world price does it propose to get in that agreement? It is now known that this year's crop was sold at a figure that is probably S100 million less than if the world market price had been obtained. Does the government propose to sell the 1948 crop at any such reduction below the world price ?
In that connection I want to refer to another section in this British wheat agreement; as a matter of fact it is part of the same section I have read. It is section 2(b), the latter part of it:
In determining the prices for these two crop years-*
Namely, the 1948 crop and the 1949 crop. -the United Kingdom government will have regard-
I hope hon. members will note these words carefully.
-the United Kingdom government will have regard to any difference between the prices paid under this agreement in the 1946-47 and 1947-48 crop years and the world prices for wheat in those years.
I should like the government to tell me what the clause means. Does it mean that in negotiating these prices before December 31, the British government is expected to pay more than world prices at that time because of the fact that it has gotten this year's crop at, say, S100 million less than the world price? Does it mean that? If not, what does it mean?
In answering that question I suggest the minister have in mind an answer given by the British Minister of Food, Hon. Mr. Stracliey, to a question in the House of Commons at AVestminster on December 11 last. It can be found in the Parliamentary Debates of the United Kingdom. The question was:
Can the right hon. gentleman explain how this policy of buying agricultural products below cost of production in the country of origin, squares with the Hot Springs resolution which
this government supported?
This is Mr. Strachey's answer:
We buy agricultural products at the lowest prices we can get them in the world, and if we deviated from that policy I am sure the house would censure us very severely indeed.
I have read the section of the British wheat agreement which says that, as to any advantage the British government now has with respect to this year's crop, the British government will have regard to it in negotiating the price to be paid for the 1948 crop. I have also read the answer made by the British minister, who, I understand, negotiated or helped to negotiate this agreement. I want now to make a brief quotation from an editorial in the Winnipeg Free Press with respect to this particular matter. The editorial is from the issue of February 27, referring to an address made by Mr. Strachey to the Canadian club in that city. I quote:
"We (the British government) do not feel that the long term interests of the United Kingdom and the British people will be served by once again seeing the prices of wheat drop to almost nothing and the wheat farmers of the world go bankrupt, one after another."
The editorial goes on:
It is hard to reconcile this with the same Air. Strachey speaking in the British House of Commons on December 11 last (Hansard, column .1156):
"We buy agricultural products at the lowest prices we can get them in the world, and if we deviated from that policy I am sure the house would censure us very severely indeed."
And in London he proceeded to argue-which should interest the farmers of the west-that bulk of state purchase-which is exemplified in the wheat agreement-is the best method of obtaining low prices.
The editorial ends with this comment:
The facts in the present case support Mr. Strachey's position at London, but not in Winnipeg-
Let me put my questions again. Does this government intend to ask the British government to pay more than the world price for the 1948 wheat crop, in view of the fact it has sold a large part of this year's crop to Britain at scores of millions of dollars less than the world price? If not, what does that section 2 (b) in the British wheat agreement mean? And what does it mean having regard to the answer given in the British House of Commons by the Hon. Mr. Strachey?
I have one other aspect of this matter to deal with, and then I shall be through. I refer to the general policy of vesting in government-appointed boards practically all the powers possessed by parliament. Under wartime powers and under the transitional powers act this government was given power to possess
Canadian Wheat Board Act

the farmer's wheat, power to sell it, power to do everything necessary to commandeer it and to direct it into certain channels. These were very wide powers. We granted them fully during the war. But in peace time parliament is placed in an invidious position. The Minister of Trade and Commerce made a long-term agreement covering wheat not yet grown. He made it nearly a year ago, for four crops. The Minister of Agriculture makes various long-term agreements about other agricultural products that are not yet produced. They are agreements to deliver farm commodities in specified amounts, and at prices fixed by the government in the agreements. The government makes the agreements and then comes to parliament and says in effect, "You must either repudiate these agreements or else give us the wide powers of compulsion that we ask for in order to carry them out."
If the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) had been in his seat today, I should have asked him if as a general principle he subscribes to legislation of that kind. I should like to have asked him, whether if he sat in the opposition instead of over there, if he were sitting here he would have let legislation of that kind be passed without protest. Almost any day now-perhaps today-we shall be discussing another bill in which similar powers will be asked for with respect to other farm products.
I should like in this connection to make our position clear. We do not recommend that any agreement already made be dishonoured. I stated that the other day. There can be no respect for governments if an international agreement entered into by one government is going to be kicked over by another, or even by itself. We do not recommend that any agreement already made be dishonoured, but we are opposed to what is rapidly becoming a general practice, namely, a minister of the crown committing this country to agreements without the approval of parliament. We are opposed to granting to a minister or to the government the power to make agreements that may change the whole face of our agriculture-that are in fact doing that-agreements which make it necessary to come to parliament and ask that unheard-of bureaucratic powers of compulsion be vested in government boards in order to carry them out. The least the government should do is to follow the practice which is followed in trade agreements, namely, to bring the agreement to parliament before it is finally ratified by any board or by any minister.
I want to read just three lines from a newspaper which, whether we agree with it or not

in all matters, has had definite views and, I think, very good views with respect to trade. On this particular matter, the Winnipeg Free Press of March 7 says:
In years to come, when Liberals recover from this kind of power madness, defacements of our statute law, like this one, will rise up to shame them.
That is all I had intended to say, Mr. Speaker, at this time. The amendment I desire to move, seconded by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Miller) is as follows:
That the said bill be not now read the third time, but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole for the purpose of reconsidering sections 20, 21 and 22 thereof.
My main purpose in referring to these particular sections is to have consideration given this one point: That the balance due on the 1945 crop, which was sown and harvested and largely sold before this agreement was entered into, be paid out now rather than included in the pool for the whole five years. I am assured that the resolution is in order. In case it should not carry, however, I should like to ask the minister or someone on the government benches to give all the information he can with respect to the balances held on the 1944 and 1945 crops, ana such information as can be given with respect to the attitude of the government in negotiating the price for next year's crop. I ask that because this session will be prorogued in midsummer and this particular business will be completed before we come back.

While I do not agree with the latter portion of the remarks of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken), I find myself pretty much in agreement with respect to the clause he wishes to have amended. As a matter of fact that was the position taken by this group in the discussion of the bill. We felt that the 1945-46 crop had been included in the agreement without the consent of the wheat producers, and that because of the rising production costs the government have permitted, which are creating a hardship at this time, the government should give serious consideration to paying out the 1945-46 participation certificates.
With regard to this matter of rising costs, we in this group have supported this bill largely because we believed the government were sincere in their intention to maintain the ceilings on the costs of production in this country. That was the undertaking the government gave this house and the country when this agreement was initiated. But we do not find that being done today. Only recently we saw the ceiling taken off gasoline and the ceiling on binder twine raised to

Canadian Wheat Board Act
permit the wholesalers to increase their prices on binder twine to the trade in western Canada by $7.50 a hundredweight. Today when the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden) asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) a question in this regard he was given a flippant answer, which shows the extent of the minister's anxiety as far as the farmers are concerned. We certainly did not appreciate that answer, and I do not think it should have been made. I do not believe he gave very much consideration to his words at that time. An increase of S7.50 a hundredweight in the price of binder twine to the western farmer means an increase of 33J per cent. That is an additional cost in the production of grain in the west, and I must say we in this group are very much disappointed in the actions of the government over the last six months, in allowing agricultural costs to increase at the rate they have increased. If this continues it will destroy the value of the whole stabilization programme as far as grains are concerned. Unless some attempt is made by the government to maintain present costs of production it is going to become a serious matter.
With regard to the amendment that has been moved, as I have said already during the discussion of the bill we suggested that this matter should be given consideration. Therefore we intend to support the amendment.

I do not consider it necessary to make a long statement at this time; I did not kiss the blarney stone when I left Ireland, so my remarks this afternoon will be brief. I simply want to say that this bill will not entirely meet with our approval, particularly in the matter of the failure of the government to give an undertaking that the wheat board will accept, at the guaranteed minimum price of $1.35, all wheat offered to it during the pool period to July 31, 1950. We feel that such a definite undertaking, expressed in plain English in this bill, should be given to the Canadian farmers. They were asked to make great sacrifices during the war. These they made with no protest whatever. They are now being asked to make further sacrifices to make possible the fulfilment of the government's agreement with Britain. It is only right, therefore, that they should be made to feel secure in the knowledge that what wheat they do raise and offer for sale during the period to July 31, 1950, will be accepted, and that at no time during the period will they be left with quantities they themselves cannot store, nor at the end of the
period with substantial quantities they may have to sell at greatly reduced prices. I listened carefully to all the arguments both for and against the proposition made from this corner of the house, and I must say I was not much impressed by the arguments of the members of the government, all of whom failed to make a valid case for their failure to give in the bill the undertaking requested by us.
Had I been a little nearer Mr. Speaker, or had his eyesight been a little better, I might have had an opportunity of moving an amendment in the following words:
That bill 23 be not now read the third time, but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole for consideration of amendments designed to commit the government to the acceptance of all wheat offered for sale during the period to July 31, 1950, to settle for the 4945 crop when sold, and to raise the initial payment to $1.55 per bushel on the four remaining crops.
Those things are what we had in mind; they are the points that were emphasized continuously during the debate, both on second reading and in committee. I hope the house will see fit to support the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) and send this bill back to committee, in order to help the farmers get a square deal even if only on this one point.
Mr. GORDON B. ISNOR (Halifax): Mr. Speaker, in rising to say a word or two in connection with this bill I wish to make it clear that I am not doing so in order to support the amendment, but rather because of the remarks made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier). I listened carefully to the discussion of this bill both in the house and in committee of the whole. Hon. members advanced arguments for and against it, and coming as I do from the east, where perhaps we are more particularly interested in fish than in wheat, it seemed to me the government was to be congratulated on having made such an agreement as this.
You probably know a lot more about fish than you do about wheat.

It is probably true that I know more about fish than I do about wheat. But after listening to the hon. member discourse for hours about wheat, I must confess I am more than ever confused as to what policy would meet his wishes, and at the same time meet those of the rest of the country.
However, after listening to arguments on all sides, it is my belief that the government has made an exceptionally good contract. I would associate myself with what was said
Canadian Wheat Board Act

oy the hon. member for St. John-Albert (Mr. Hazen) who, the day before yesterday, brought to the government's attention the fact that wheat was being shipped through United States ports. We in the east were conscious of this as early as last October. As a result, at that time the Halifax board of trade, acting in conjunction with the board of trade of the city of Saint John, brought to the attention of the government, and particularly the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon), their fear of a shortage of wheat on the Atlantic coast, thereby making it almost impossible for the government to carry out its commitment.
I would repeat that it was as early as last October that we brought this matter to the attention of the government, and particularly to the attention of the Department of Transport and the Department of Trade and Commerce. Today the Minister of Transport has given figures showing the number of box cars which were in the United States, and also in eastern and western Canada. I shall not deal with this in detail, more than to say that had the railways been alive to the situation, as it was brought to their attention last October, and in the following months of November and December, the shortage of 8,000 box cars in Canada today would not exist.
In support of his contention the minister has urged that it was necessary to ship through the United States port of Portland, and has stated that, while the box car turn-back from Portland was four days, it was eight days from Halifax. In stating that, however, he forgot an important fact in his picture of the transportation system. I refer to the shipping distance from Halifax.
At this point I should like to place some figures on record. The sailing time of a 16-knot vessel from London to Montreal is 203 hours, while to Saint John it is 182 hours and, to Halifax, 172 hours. Halifax is thus ten hours shorter than Saint John and thirty-one hours shorter than Montreal. Then, it need not be repeated that Halifax is open all the year round, so far as shipping is concerned, and at all times is entirely free of ice.
Can the hon. member tell us the number of hours from Portland?
There is no question in my mind that grain shipped through Halifax would reach London much faster than if it were shipped through Portland.
About six hours.

Thank you. In addition to that I have in mind the additional employment resulting from shipment through Cana-

dian ports. Last year, when export-import legislation was before the house I pointed out that at the port of Halifax we have 1,600 longshoremen, 1,000 freight handlers and 1,400 others more or less directly connected with the handling of cargo at our port.
Then, it is not only grain with which we are concerned. The bringing of ships to our ports to handle grain has the effect of creating other cargoes, thus adding to the number of ships entering our ports, and to the amount of business derived from those ships by way of repairs and other employment in connection therewith. Every time a ship of 5,000 tons is loaded or unloaded at Halifax it means that an average of $12,500 is paid out in wages.
I now come to the question of the shipment of grain through the port of Halifax. In 1942 there were 32,844,580 bushels shipped through that port. In 1945 that figure had dropped to 15,051,638, and this year it is estimated that no more than 7,000,000 bushels will be shipped through Halifax.
One can understand my concern with respect to the failure to make arrangements for the transportation of grain through Canadian ports, and my further concern that no consideration, so far as I know, has been give to including in the wheat agreement a provision which would definitely guarantee that all grain for export should be shipped through Canadian ports. When I refer to Canadian ports I am referring not only to that great port of Halifax, but to all ports of Canada.
It will be recalled that the late Right Hon. W. S. Fielding made a special provision to the extent of ten per cent in favour of goods entering through Canadian ports, and I should like to see a provision something along that line in this agreement. Therefore I suggest to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), through you, Mr. Speaker, that, in addition to the sections already appearing in the bill, he add another stating:
And it is further agreed that all goods under this contract or agreement must be shipped through Canadian ports.
I do not wish unnecessarily to take up the time of the house in the discussion of this measure. I felt, however, that I must say a word in connection with transportation, particularly in view of the fact that some of us in the east recognized away back as early as October, 1946, that a situation such as has arisen might develop. It is because of the present condition that I urge the government today to consider the views I have expressed, and to see that no further shipments pass through United States ports, but rather that

Canadian Wheat Board Act
in future they pass through our own Canadian ports, thus adding to employment at those points.
The hon. member for St. John-Albert stated that a million bushels of wheat had been shipped through Portland. I think the figure of one million bushels is used for that particular period, and I am concerned over the possibility of there being further shipments of a similar quantity. I hope the Minister of Agriculture will take these views of mine into consideration and pass them along to the Minister of Transport in order to make sure that we do not have to put up with this sort of thing.

tion with the United States loan. I support the motion made by the leader of the opposition to refer this bill back to the committee. I believe it should be referred back and considered very carefully. Great Britain did so much for us during the war, and we should not fail to support the mother country in the great food, coal and electricity crises which face her today.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is necessary to restate the position of the C.C.F. in connection with this bill or to point out what we consider are the inadequacies of the legislation. This has been done very well by my colleagues who spoke on the second reading, but there are some observations which I should like to make. I agree in principle with the bill; but, as has been mentioned, it is not adequate. In the past we have seen great fluctuations in farm prices, and in this connection I wish to refer to a newspaper report as follows:
Mr. Hannam quoted Fiorello LaGuardia, New York, as saying: "You know and I know that the farmers of the world have been exploited and are still being exploited."
Then Mr. Hannam continued:
We want stability not for purely selfish reasons. We want it if the people of the world are going to have more and better food to eat.
That is one of the great considerations at this time. It has been said that this bill affects only Canada, but I maintain that it affects all the world and, because of that, it is one of the most important bills coming up in this house.
We attempted to give some sort of stability to agriculture during the war, but the government permitted a break in the stability when they allowed an increase in prices of farm machinery. That was nearly the straw which breaks the camel's back, because, for the first time, we had farmers organizing to put on a non-delivery strike. If this sort of thing continues and the government does not accept the responsibility for giving parity prices to agriculture, rather than stability in the basement, we shall have a situation in Canada which will be a reflection on democracy in this country.
The farmers of western Canada are not satisfied with this agreement. We feel that we should have parity; that we should have a decent standard of living; that we should have prices above the cost of production which will guarantee us a decent standard of living. The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker) was quoted in the press and he can correct me if I am wrong; before the opening of the session he was reported as having said

that he was coming here to ask for $1.85 wheat. I wish to say-and I intend to say it to my farmers and constituents-I do not think you can have your cake and eat it. If you want stability you must be ready to accept a price of parity. In other words, at the moment you cannot demand the world price which is perhaps enhanced by world conditions, and immediately afterwards demand parity. But I do say that, unless we go back to the 1900 economics and administration of government, today the government should, take the responsibility to see that agriculture gets parity.
What has happened is that during the war the farmers have taken losses on their wheat. In most cases our prices have been steady and stabilized. As was indicated by one hon. member, the farmers have lost money which they could have received. If our farm products, chiefly wheat, were sold on world markets we could have received around $400 million. However the farmers were not kicking so much until the cost of production started to go up. As was intimated in the house today by the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden), the restrictions on the ceiling price of gasoline will be removed the last of the month. We find that the price of binder twine is going up. In the face of that, we find that the responsible minister has the audacity to rise in his place and say, without any show of seriousness, that these matters are being given the usual consideration, or something to that effect. If that is the usual consideration which is being given to the difficult problems in this country I want to say that we are headed for another depression which will be as bad as the one we had in 1930 when the Tories were in power.
I believe we have come farther than that. I should like to indicate to the government that, although we have had in the west a degree of prosperity, yet this situation prevails. I hold in my hand statistics which were furnished me by the bureau of statistics. These statistics show that the total farm debt, including mortgages and agreements of sale of land for the year 1941, stood at $799 million, and further that the institutional holdings of farm debt by insurance companies, trust loans on mortgages, government agencies, municipalities, railways and so forth in 1938 stood at $418 million. By 1945 when we had been getting decent prices and good crops we had reduced that debt to $263 million. But I wish to point out that, until that debt is practically cleared up and the farmers get out of the red, we want fair prices for the

Canadian Wheat Board Act
farmers. This indicates that our whole economy is going out of gear and we are headed for a position where we shall have decreased consumption. What we farmers want is everyone. to have all they want to eat.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) said that, until beef was rationed in this country, we had not shipped any considerable amount of beef out and that we had to continue rationing because we had put
750,000	of our boys and girls in the services. They were starting to have some money in their pockets and our farmers were starting to get decent prices and putting beef on their tables as they had not done before. This indicates that there is a potential market in Canada. Only when the people get a fair share of the national income, good wages and fair prices will they buy that stuff.
I was talking to a friend of mine in this city the other day. He was in a butcher shop where he usually does his buying, and the butcher said to him as a lady came in- they were speaking about the business trends which were taking place-"Watch what that lady buys." He said: "Formerly, three weeks ago she would have bought a Saturday night order of around $12 worth of the best cuts of meat in my shop." She bought bologna and some of the cheaper cuts of meat. That is what is going on. She bought only $2 worth. That is what is taking place all over the country today.
The "Economic Annalist" of February, 1946, states this:
The cash income from the sale of farm products for 1945 is estimated by the bureau of statistics at $1,654 million. This total is about 8 per cent less than the record high of 1944.
I hold in my hand a press report of the remarks of George Bickerton, publicity director of the United Farmers of Canada, Saskatchewan section, which says:
Saskatchewan farmers' income dropped $137,-
573,000	in 4945 with a further drop of $50,485,000, in the first six months of 1946.
That is the situation which faces us today. We of this group have asked for the inclusion in this bill of all coarse grains, but we have been unable to have that done. I might point out that flak, which I think all hon. members will recognize is one of the crops which we should have produced on a stable basis over the years and not on a fluctuating production basis, in 1941 brought an average price per bushel, No. 1, at Fort William and Port Arthur of $1,615. By 1945 it was $2.75 a bushel. This shows that in many parts of agricultural production there is no stability whatsoever.
We are not completely satisfied with this bill. In the first place, I believe that all participation dividends and sales coming from the 1945 crop should be paid out for that year. It is the responsibility of this government how they do it. That is their business, but we should have from year to year calculated parity prices for the farmers. I support the motion of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) that sections 20, 21 and 22 be referred back to the committee for further consideration.

I shall be brief. I have taken it for granted that the responsible minister for the department and the responsible minister for the United Kingdom-Canada wheat agreement would have endeavoured to answer the questions which were put so frankly and forthrightly by my leader in his discussion this afternoon. I just wish to say-
May I just suggest that if the minister spoke he would close the debate.

On a point of order, is it not true that if the minister speaks a second time he will close the debate? He has moved third reading and has therefore spoken once. If he speaks again will he not be speaking twice?
Mr. DEPI T\ SPEAKER: I would remind the house that we are now discussing the amendment. There is no closing of the debate on an amendment.
Then the minister has spoken.
