That is so.

As I said, I had contemplated waiting until the two responsible ministers had endeavoured to answer the questions put by my leader. Since they sat silent and Your Honour was prepared to put the motion, I thought I should make a few brief remarks.
Referring to the amendment which was moved by my leader, I wish to say that when the producers of Canada planned their operations for the production of wheat during 1945 they were distinctly led to believe by the government of the day that they would receive an initial payment and participation
Canadian Wheat Board Act

I wish to make a comment or two on the question before the house. It seems to me that the field has narrowed down considerably since the question of the wheat board act first came up. It appears now that we are in disagreement with the bill because it does not provide certain benefits for the farmer. This afternoon the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) repeated what he has said before in this house, that is, that he is not opposed to living up to the terms of the British wheat agreement. In other words, we are now assured that, regardless of who the government shall be in the next few succeeding years, the wheat agreement will hold.
The leader of the opposition has always said that.

That is what I am saying. Furthermore, we find that the leader of the opposition has moved an amendment which would refer the bill back to the committee for reconsideration of sections 20, 21 and 22, and by implication this means that he is in complete agreement with the bill except for those sections. That now narrows the field down considerably to the question of what is contained in these three sections. I think the biggest bone of contention now is not the principle of the bill as a whole but whether
the farmer, under the bill, is getting all the benefits he should get out of it and getting them at the right time. The two things under discussion at the present time appear to be the payment of participation benefits and the initial price of the wheat itself. I think both those problems can be combined and can be easily solved if the proper minister would rise in his place in this house and say today that the initial price of wheat shall be $1.55 instead of $1.35. By making that announcement he would be doing two things. First, he would be guaranteeing the farmer a greater immediate income on his grain; and, second, he would be leaving far less money in the wheat board fund, over which the argument seems to be developing; that is to say, there would be less left for distribution at the end of the pool period and more money would be made available immediately to the farmers.
I do not think any argument has been brought forward in this house to prove that the government could not pay $1.55 as an initial price; and the trend of events in the last few months alone is such that we are being forced to the conclusion that, unless the government is willing to pay more for the grain or else to hold the price of other commodities down, the very basis on which this British wheat agreement could have been successful will be completely destroyed. The farmers who accepted the agreement did so because they felt that there was a real need overseas for as much food as possible at prices as reasonable as possible in this period of time. What we see happening around us now is that the government is permitting price ceilings to be lifted and washed out entirely, and the price is jumping, as the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) just quoted, as high as eighty per cent on binder twine. We do not know what the new price will be on gasoline, but we know it will not be less; it is going to be more. In the face of that, the government is now put in the position of responsibility of having to do one of two things, either make a real effort to hold prices down

in fact, it would be necessary now to roll them back-or else to increase the benefits the farmer is to receive under this bill. If one of those two things is not done, the farmers have a legitimate complaint and the government will get a rude awakening in a very short period of time.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendment which has been moved would have to be changed in its wording, I think, before it
Canadian Wheat Board Act

would really mean anything at all in connection with the bill itself. The amendment says that the said bill be not now read the third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole for the purpose of reconsidering sections 20, 21 and 22 thereof. There are only six sections of this bill. There are no sections 20, 21 and 22. Therefore there would have to be added to the amendment, in order to make it mean what it is intended to mean, "included in clause 5 thereof". That is, these sections referred to are sections of the wheat board act which are included in clause 5 of this particular bill, and the wording would have to be changed in order to provide for that.
But before the vote is taken, there are a number of things which I should like to say with regard to the discussion which has taken place. We have had a long discussion on the three points which have been raised : the question as to whether we should increase the initial payment; whether the participation for 1945 should be paid out at once rather than be made part of the five-year pool, and, further, whether the government should announce definitely that all the wheat would be taken by July 31, 1950; that is, all the wheat that is presented to the government would be taken or would be paid for at $1.35 a bushel as an initial price.
As I was saying a moment ago, those three questions I think took up most of the time of the discussion in committee. There was very little discussion on anything else. We discussed those questions continuously, first, under section 17 of the wheat board act and, later, under sections 20, 21 and 22 of the act which, as I said a moment ago, are included in clause 5 of this bill. In discussing those matters, I think every point of view which could be expressed in the committee, if it were referred back again, was expressed then; and the committee finally gave its consent to the provisions of those three sections.
I do not know whether I should repeat very much of what was said or of what I myself said on that occasion; but in view of some of the remarks which have been made, I think that certain arguments should be repeated. In the first place, if we were to follow to its logical conclusion the action which is now proposed, and if the bill itself were not acceptable to the government on the terms that are suggested, and the bill were defeated, then of course the whole principle of the bill would be defeated just as effectively on third reading as it would be on second reading; particularly if the bill had gone back to the committee, had been reported again for third reading with terms the same as

they are now, and were defeated in the house. If we went on with that to its logical conclusion we would succeed in defeating the principle of the bill and defeating the bill itself.
Those who belong to the official opposition have been insisting, ever since this session opened, that controls should be got rid of. Some have even gone so far as to suggest that it should not be in any orderly manner. Some controls have been got rid of. Some ceilings have been taken off. I should1 like to suggest that I believe the farm organizations of this country meant what they said when they said they were in favour of stabilization. I believe, too, if we are not satisfied, as farm organizations, to give sufficient time for the carrying out of any orderly changes which must be made in connection with price levels, there is only one thing which can result, and that is that action finally will have to be taken in a disorderly manner.
Just by way of illustration, may I remind hon. members that a week or ten days ago, after strong pressure over a long period of time, action was taken to remove what I think was at least an inconvenience-and perhaps one oould use an even stronger term-resulting from the fact that wheat was supplied to the people of this country at a lower price than that at which it was supplied to Britain, and-this at the expense of the farmer. Action was taken in regard to that matter, and along with it action was taken which resulted in an increase in the price of feed wheat. This, of course, had two results, one being to give the producer of wheat a higher return, and the other to increase the cost to farmers in certain sections of Canada using that wheat for feed. Immediately exception was taken to the fact that an increased cost had been caused the poultry and egg producers, and it was therefore argued that there should be an increase in the price of eggs. As a matter of fact, a few months earlier the floor price of eggs had been increased by one cent a dozen over about half the year and by two cents a dozen over the other half, while no change was made in the price of feed. That was done by increasing the price under the British agreement by that amount. Now it is argued that when the cost of feed is put up again there must be a further increase in the price of eggs. Probably within certain limits that contention is justifiable, but certainly it is not reasonable to suggest that no consideration whatever should be given the fact that the price of eggs was increased at a time when the price of feed was not increased.	.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
On the other hand, today we had the fact brought up that the ceiling has been raised on binder twine. Some have said this represents an increase of eighty per cent in the price of that commodity. I am not in a position to say just what the increase will be in the price of binder twine, but I know that, with the situation existing in the world in relation to the material from which binder twine is made, if we were to have any binder twine at all some decision with respect to that matter had to be made in March. If we are to have binder twine in July and August to harvest the crops across this country, then a decision in the matter had to be made by March at least, and very early in the month. That is one reason the decision has been made at this time.
For the last two or three weeks hon. members have been quite properly pressing for a statement in the house in regard to the returns that are to be provided, under control, on feed grains. At the time of the conference last December it was suggested that if all the controls relating to food products and feed were to be retained through the crop year 1947-48, a certain procedure should be followed. There are present today a few who were also present at the conference of last December between representatives of the provinces, the farm organizations and the federal Department of Agriculture. They will remember that before Mr. Wesson proceeded to present his idea that an acreage payment of S5 might be made, he asked the definite question of the chair as to whether it was the intention of the government to continue those controls throughout the crop year 1947-48. That question was referred to me, as a member of the government. At that time I stated I was not in a position to say definitely what would be done with regard to prices throughout the year 1947-48, but that if we were to continue to attempt to fulfil our agreements with Great Britain to deliver farm products at the prices set out in .those agreements, leaving out the question of quantities altogether, it would be necessary to have some form of control throughout the crop year 1947-48. In the discussions which followed it was stated definitely that the subsidy of $5 per acre would or could be decided upon only if an attempt was to be made to hold prices at the Levels then existing, because immediately you allowed them to change, the whole situation would change. So the proposal itself was based upon the idea that price levels were to be maintained.
Since that time, as has been indicated by some of the steps taken, the government has 83166-86
concluded that prices cannot be maintained throughout the whole crop year 1947-48 at the levels in existence at the time those discussions took place; and because they cannot be maintained, certain actions have to be taken from time to time. If we are to handle the situation in an orderly fashion I believe we must expect that those who are presumed to benefit by the controls which are being retained should at least have sufficient patience to permit the action taken to progress to the point where all sides of the question may be examined. In connection with binder twine, I said a moment ago that if we did not act early in March we would not have any binder twine. From remarks which have been made I assume that when the minister this afternoon made the short reply that this question had been given the usual careful consideration before a decision was reached, it was not considered by many hon. members to be a sufficient explanation under the circumstances.
Not in view of the manner in which it was said.

Well, I am simply discussing the facts which I know are apparent to farmers. Every farmer knows that the substance from which binder twine is made must come a great distance, and that there has been some difficulty in obtaining quantities of that material for the purpose of providing binder twine both during and since the war. So action had to be taken early.
May I ask if any British companies supply us with large amounts of sisal?

I am not in a position to answer that question offhand, though perhaps the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) or the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) might be able to do so. In any event, arrangements have to be made to obtain certain quantities of this material, and whether they are made with the government or with a company they must be made well in advance.

Is it not true there
are large supplies of binder twine already in Canada upon which subsidy has been paid?

There would be some; I do not know how much. However the figure can be obtained. There would be some here. But whether there is some here, and no matter how much there is here, there will have to be more binder twine supplied before the harvest season.
Canadian Wheat Board Act

The price has been
maintained because of the subsidy paid by the government; is that not true?

Yes, that is right, up
to the present time. And I should say that two ministers have said, prior to discussion in committee-and I referred to it while we were in committee-that subsidies were on the way out, and that the tendency was to try to incorporate subsidies into prices; a procedure which I think a great many people would desire to have followed, and to have completed at as early a date as possible.
And in doing that, of course, in connection with farm products movement has to be taken at the time it is wise to do so. Let me go back to the illustration with respect to eggs. We were making our agreement with Great Britain last fall. That was the time we had to consider rising prices of eggs. Then we were considering the matter of giving the farmer of western Canada the treatment to which he was entitled in connection with flour supplied here, and we decided that the time to deal with that was in the latter part of January.
I suppose the two things could have been done at one time, but there are reasons why it was difficult to do them at one time. Probably the proper time to deal with eggs, so far as future treatment is concerned, would be in April or May; and until we have reached that time it is difficult to make changes in the situation which now exists. Those changes will come about in the proper course of events.
The feed grain decision was something I was not able to announce prior to today, and I am sorry to say I am not in a position to announce it today. As I said yesterday, I had hoped I would be able to announce it at the end of the week, and I pointed out that the end of the week was Friday. But I find, after discussion which took place today, that there is a desire on the part of some of those who have to put these changes into effect, to have the week-end in which to discuss them with some of their men, who are in Winnipeg, rather than Ottawa. That is, they are men connected with the wheat board itself. Therefore it may be necessary to hold over the announcement until Monday.
I am sure, however, that if I could make that announcement now, and compare it with what has been done in connection with binder twine, every farmer in this country would agree that far more has been done to increase returns on grain than has been taken from him by anything that has been done in connection with binder twine.

Does the minister
include gasoline and tractor distillate, also?

One would want to
know what will happen in connection with tractor oil and distillate. But I am told this, that at least in some parts of Canada gasoline has not been selling up to the ceiling recently. And if it has not been selling up to the ceiling recently, I do not know any reason why it would sell over the ceiling, at least in those parts of Canada, if the ceiling were taken off.
That is one of the facts which was before the government at the time the matter was discussed; and I venture to say there are many members in the house who will agree that when a shift is being made from one position to another, the time to make it is when it is least likely to impose any additional cost on those who have to buy the commodity.
I know no individual can guess these things accurately, and be able to say that there is no chance in the world of prices going up. I would not attempt to say that at this time. But one has to decide on the time to make these decisions, and to make them in a manner which will at least give the least possibility of costs going where they are not intended to go.
I bring out these facts in order to say this, again, that if we are to be able to hold the line at all, in the stabilization of prices, either by the action of this house or in any other way, then we cannot be changing our minds every few days or every few hours with regard to whether we support the principle behind a piece of legislation, or whether by our action or our words we support the views and the desires of those who are out to kill this legislation, by every means that is available to them to do it. And as regards any means which result in switching this legislation backwards and forwards from this house to a committee, and from the committee to the house, and then over to the senate, and back into the committee, and then out of the committee and into the senate, and then back to this house, with changes made; if this legislation or any other legislation to establish stabilized prices for farmers has to go through all that kind of thing, then I say that there will not be very much in the way of stabilization that will ever get past this parliament.
If we are to establish stabilized prices for farmers at all, then I think we must decide upon the principle we intend to drive for, and then we must continue to drive for it. We should not depart from that principle simply because those who have been fighting the legislation from the beginning, those who have

Canadian Wheat Board Act
opposed the wheat agreement from the time it was first announced, now suggest that we should do something about the matter; rather we should continue to support those who have fought for the principle throughout and have attempted to put it on the statute books of this country.
Something was said with regard to the action of Mr. Strachey while he was speaking in the House of Commons in Great Britain, and while he was in Winnipeg. Some suggestion has been made to the effect that Mr. Strachey could not have been right both times. Well, when Mr. Strachey was speaking on the floor of the House of Commons in Great Britain he was answering a general question put to him with regard to food products.
Danish, particularly.

Yes. And in answering that question dealing, as has been suggested, largely with Danish food products, products coming from a country with which considerations such as those existing between Great Britain and Canada have not been entered into at all, he gave a certain answer. But when he was in the city of Winnipeg he was dealing with a specific question, namely the question of wheat, as covered by this bill. And in everything he said at Winnipeg he gave the impression to the people of this country that the undertakings given in the wheat agreement would be carried out in spirit, as well as in the letter. I think we should accept those opinions as those of the minister who signed the contract, or at least was here just prior to its being signed-one of his officials signed it-and the minister who took part in the discussions.
The Winnipeg Free Press has been quoted. Well, Mr. Speaker, I have not taken time out during these discussions to say very much about the Winnipeg Free Press, because I am not worried at all about whether the Free Press wants to put itself in the position of being a local newspaper instead of a national one. If that is what they desire to have themselves considered, then that is quite all right with me. They are speaking, or have been speaking, in, connection with this matter, for a group for whom I do not blame them for speaking. That is their own choice. But I have in my hand some articles which appeared in another paper owned and published by the same people in the city of Saskatoon, the Star-Phoenix. These four articles deal with the wheat agreement. One could take not only the articles which appeared on the editorial page, but the editorials of the editorial writer who is answering the editor of the Winnipeg Free Press, who is also 83166-864
answering the assistant associate editor of the Winnipeg Free Press, and answering them most effectively.
Who is the author of those articles?
Mr. Richardson is the editor of the paper, and I have no doubt he takes responsibility for what appears on the editorial page. His name is not on the articles, but he writes the editorials.
What is their date?

The first one is dated January 20, 1947. It reads:
The Canadian wheat agreement with Great Britain cannot be judged fairly aside from the general trade outlook and the problems of restoring international trade.
And farther down:
A simple test, which may be applied with profit to other proposals, practices and policies-affecting trade, is whether it facilitates or retards the reopening of trade channels that were closed or impaired by the war. One further test might be applied: Does it prejudice the future expansion of international trade? Plainly it does not prejudice the future. Section 7 of me agreement says that "its terms and conditions shall be subject to any modification or amendment which may be necessary to bring it into conformity with any international agreements or arrangements hereafter entered into to which both governments are parties."
Then he goes on:
The merit of lending funds to overseas customers in order to stimulate our trade requires no explanation. The alternative is to shut down our production to the narrow limits required to export only to those who have Canadian dollars.
He goes on to support that action, and then he says:
The Canadian wheat agreement has stood the test, as we may now see it in the perspective of several months experience with it. It has given economic and psychological assurance to our best wheat customer.
May I say that the editor of this paper spent a considerable part of the war years in London. He continues:
Without it, the series of crises which were inevitable in the economic rehabilitation of Britain would have been deepened undoubtedly by an unbearable austerity in the British diet, which has been almost unbearable as it is! Without it, the opportunity of leadership in the economic reconstruction of western Europe, which only Britain can exercise, would have' been denied at a time when default could leave only chaos and invite the commercial isolationism which serves as the economic policy of communism. The door was half open, in any case. Discussions of -the wheat agreement without taking account of these vital aspects of the world trade situation in the present transition will serve only to obscure the purpose -and definition of all our_ future hopes. The agreement has been a main bridge between two worlds which
Canadian Wheat Board Act

can be integrated permanently by the reconstruction of world trading facilities. Without such bridges, even now all talk of an international trade convention would be little than idle speculation within the rigid walls oi an isolated dollar area in which Canada s destiny would steadily darken.
As I say, that is another paper published by the same people who publish the Winnipeg Free Press. It gives me the idea that the editorial policy of their papers is the editorial policy of the individual who writes the editorials. That was always so when the late John Dafoe was editor of the Winnipeg Free Press. No one during that period of time ever considered that he was expressing the opinions of anyone but John Dafoe. I venture to say that the time will come when no one will consider that this young editor is expressing the opinion of anyone but himself when he is writing views which affect all the people of this country. He goes on to say:
Since the Canadian wheat agreement with Great Britain was announced last July, the main criticisms made against it have become clear. On the one hand, the charge that Canada had broken its pledged word to the United States to work for the removal of discrimination in trade was quickly exploded.
He goes on to answer that charge. May I say again, that the editor of this paper spent the latter part of the war in Britain and that he spent part of it in Washington, and the part which he did not spend1 in either Washington or London was spent in Ottawa. He has some knowledge as to what these questions mean.
A moment ago the minister spoke of "this young editor." Does he refer to the editor of the Winnipeg Free Press?

No; the editor of the Star-Phoenix, Mr. Richardson. He ends with these words:
It is now said in Britain that the worst is over, though it is not all line sailing jet. lhe Canadian wheat agreement has made an mcalcul-able contribution to this result, which is m Canada's own best interests as a wheat exporter. It is serving to bridge the transition, it has stimulated the revival of world trade under new and strange conditions. Even more happily, it has brought us nearer the goal which we will reach only by going forward with the Americans and the British into an era of freer trade.
That sums up the opinion which the writer of the articles in the Star-Phoenix has with regard to the Winnipeg Free Press. This man writing in the Star-Phoenix takes the view that the opinions held by the Winnipeg Free Press are not correct. He has the courage to state what his views are with regard to the matter.

After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Britain has always agreed that over a period of time our prices should be stabilized in a reasonable relationship to the prices which the farmers receive for food to be consumed in Britain off the farms of Britain, and I am confident t that, as we go along, the answer to the question asked by the leader of the opposition with regard to 1948 will be made apparent to everyone in this house.
The leader of the opposition asked, what is the government to ask for in 1948; what is the government to ask for in 1949. Hon. members know what has been stated on previous occasions, namely that the British have agreed that there shall be no ceiling on what we may ask for in the last two years; and the fact that there is no ceiling on what we may ask for in those last two years should be an answer to the question that has been posed: Are you going to ask as much as the world market offers at that time for wheat? Obviously, if the world market remains as high as it is now, which very few expect, there will be no reason for asking less than the world price in the third year of the contract. If the world price is lower than SI.55, obviously there will be reason for asking a higher price than the world price is at that time. The question as to how much will be obtained as a result of what is asked is something no one in this house can answer at the present time. We simply rely on the fact that in all dealings we have had with Britain throughout the war, prior to the war, and since the war, the indications have been that we can depend upon the letter and spirit of the agreement that we have with them, not only with regard to wheat but as respects other products.
I am sorry to interrupt the right hon. gentleman but his time has expired.
This is an important matter, Mr. Speaker, and the minister should be allowed to proceed.

I have no desire to
continue if my time is up. At any rate, there is only one further argument that I care to make on the subject. An appeal has been made for a statement of the position in relation to payments which are already made and which are to be made on the different years, and the suggestion has been made that there was an understanding with the farmers that participation would be paid annually throughout the period. I am not going to argue the question again as to whether the period was intended to be five years or four years. I think it is well understood by every

farm organization in Canada and all leaders of farm organizations, and by everyone else who has ever discussed the matter, that the five-year period existed before the British wheat contract existed at all. It was suggested this afternoon that, after the wheat contract had been entered into, the decision was reached to make the term a five-year one. The five-year term was presented in this house in September, 1945, and it always was a five-year term. There never was any suggestion that it be otherwise until all the terms of the British agreement were known; and then, as I stated the other night, that suggestion in the first instance came from the government and not from farm organizations. But after the discussion was completed, it was concluded that the 1945 crop would be retained in the pool.
I said something the other day which apparently did not register with the committee, when we were discussing this same question in committee. I stated that I did not see how this or any other government could retain in the treasury of Canada two or three hundred million dollars which belonged to some group of citizens in this country, mentioning particularly the farmers. If we had in the treasury of Canada in, let us say. 1948, as a result of the fact that prices remained high, two. three or four hundred million dollars, no government in Canada could carry that money through until the end of the contract. There would be a constant demand for the money to be paid out to the people to whom it belonged, and there would be an inclination on the part of any government that was in office under those circumstances to make an interim payment, just as an interim payment was made under similar circumstances when the wheat pools were in existence. But to say at this stage that, no matter what happens to be in the treasury, interim payment will be made, would be to take an impossible position in relation to the whole matter.
Will the minister state that he will not make that payment before an election?

Of course, if my hon. friends all get together some time, they can determine that payment is not made until after an election. I should like to suggest that if they want an election on an issue of that kind, it is not a bad thing from our point of view to have it on. '

The Minister of Agriculture had one try-out on it.

May I suggest to members of the house that when the hon. gentleman who was fortunate enough to win that election to which reference is made, came into this house and made his first speech, he did not even mention the British wheat contract. He knew what he won the election on. I, too, know what he won the election on. He is too good a campaigner to think he won the election on the British wheat contract or anything related to it.
How much money have you? That is a simple question.
I shall leave it to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon), whose bill this is, to state how much we have.
Will he do that?

Yes, he will state how much we have. But what I want to point out to members of the house is this. If we had a large amount, no government could retain it in the treasury. It would require to be paid out as we went along. But if we were down in the position where there was some question as to whether we were going to take losses, then it would be absolutely impossible to make a payment. I think it would be inadvisable to make a payment from the point of view of the farmer himself, and the farmer would realize that.
Coming to the question which was in the mind of the leader of the opposition this afternoon and apparently is still in the mind of the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith), as to how much money we have, all I am going to say at this moment is that when the Minister of Trade and Commerce gives the amount I venture to say that every member of this house will be surprised at how small it is, not at how big it is. The payment of ten cents a bushel, which is already paid on 1945 or is being paid, reduces the amount to a figure which I think will be found by this house to be surprisingly low. I am not going to attempt to give that offhand. It is on record and will be given a little later.
Oh, come on; tell us.

The position in relation to the matter and in relation to the whole principle underlying not only this bill but
the other agreements which will come down under the farm products bill, is being battled in Canada at the present time. The battle against that principle is being led, naturally, by the leader of the opposition in this house. Those who support the opposite view with regard to this principle will, of course, vote against a measure of this kind or will vote against the agreements that are covered in the other bill. But I venture to say that when the vote is taken-as it will be shortly-on this question, it will again be found that the government has the support of the majority of the members upon the policy which is now before the house.
The vote on the third reading is just as much a vote for or against the policy or principle of a bill as the vote on the second reading. I venture to say that the whole principle of this bill is bound up in the three sections which we are being asked to refer back to the committee. While there may be some things that individual members disagree about with regard to the details of what is contained in those sections, I am quite satisfied that a vote for the third reading of the bill at this time will strengthen the idea in the minds of the people of Canada that this principle of stabilizing prices for farmers at a reasonable level, with a guarantee that any profit which is made over and above that reasonable level will be turned over to the farmer in due course, is a principle which the farmers of this country desire to have and which this house ought to express itself decisively upon.

Mr. Speaker, I am quite sure that everybody in this house knows perfectly well where this party stands regarding matters of this description. I do not think I need reiterate what we have so often said in this house, that we desire to see proper, orderly marketing and proper price stability at a proper level for the producers of this country. We do not wish to go back again to the days before the war, when prices went sky-high, as they did some years ago, and which were followed by a period of low prices when, as the British minister of food put it the other day, wheat was the value of chaff. However I must say this. When the British agreement which is connected with this bill was before the house last August, we made it perfectly clear that our support for that agreement and the method adopted by the government to implement the agreement through the wheat board was in no small measure connected with a continuance of the
Canadian Wheat Board Act

policy of the government as it was being carried out regarding controls and price ceilings. In the past six months costs of production have risen and the cost of living has risen. In the month of January of this year, according to the index-which of course does not comprise a very wide field of commodities-the cost of living increase was eight-tenths of one per cent in one month; or, put on the basis of the year, approximately 9A per cent for one month. If the government removes controls and lifts price ceilings to the extent that the cost of living rises and costs of production rise, then of course the basis of the British wheat agreement and the payments that are now being made to our farming community are neither fair nor just.
I would remind the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) that on August 15 last, speaking on the British wheat agreements, as reported at page 4825 of Hansard for that day, I said:
... at the present time the wheat agreement calls for the payment of $1.55 a bushel for the wheat that is sold to Britain, and I believe that is nearer what we sometimes eall a parity price. I believe the government would be well advised to consider the suggestion that, in the event of the costs of production rising for the next few years, as they will do largely because of the government's failure to maintain the ceilings, any difference there may be between what the farmer receives for his wheat and the increased costs of production should be made up out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada.
Not even out of the five-year pool that was being established. I went on to develop that a little, and the Minister of Agriculture admitted in reply that at that time-and I use his own words-parity would probably be about $1.41 or $1.42, and that the farmers' organizations had argued for $1.40 as the basic price. Then there was some discussion between the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken), the Minister of Agriculture and myself, and the minister went on to say, dealing with the matter of the compensatory fund which I had suggested:
What I want to point out is that under the floor price measure-that is not the proper name, but it will do-we stated to the house that $200,000,000 was being provided for the purpose of taking care of any adjustments in connection with what might be known as parity on other farm products. At the same time we stated to the house that similar arrangements would be made if necessary, through the wheat board, in connection with grain.
The point I am making is that if the government allows price ceilings to be lifted and costs of production to rise as they have risen, then it is the obligation of the government to provide compensation to the farmers who have accepted this wheat agreement and the

prices that go with it. I know the minister is perfectly correct when he says that in this country at the present time there is a group of people who want to upset this wheat agreement and every other agreement of this description because they have an economic interest in doing so. I have stated several times in this house that I believe the policy of the government in regard to stabilized prices and negotiated agreements, under the conditions that exist at the present time, is the best policy for Canada and the farmers of Canada. No one who attended the food and agriculture meeting at Copenhagen-I did not attend, but I have read the record of proceedings-or who sat in, as I did, at commission No. 2 of the united nations organization and heard the discussion regarding food, can be under any illusion for a moment but that this is the only kind of agreement which at this moment will adequately protect the producers of this country. The Monetary Times makes it very clear that this campaign is being carried on. If you look at the issue for February, 1947, under the heading, "Wheat Agreement," on page 42 you will find:
Speaking of the west recalls the wheat agreement with the U.K. Usually, after an arrangement like this is sanctioned by parliament for a term of years, the opposition lets up and those protesting become resigned to "taking" it. Not so in this case. The opposition of the grain trade is as tenacious today as if the agreement were before parliament. The opposition of the Progressive Conservative leader, Mr. Bracken, is equally so.
That is quite true. We are interested in one point especially in particular regarding this agreement. When this bill was before the house and in committee, on numerous occasions my colleagues raised this point, and I myself raised it just before the vote was taken, that I did not think it was proper or is proper to put the proceeds of the 1945 crop into this pool. That is the main point at issue, which we feel needs to be dealt with by the government. We realize what the minister says, that if a very large accumulation of funds is to be found in this pool within the next two or three years, no government in Canada could hold back those funds from the real owners, but I suggest that the 1945 crop payment should not have been connected with the British agreement. If we could get a satisfactory promise that this matter would be reconsidered we have otherwise very little criticism of the bill, though, as I have indicated in what I have said already, we would have liked to see the initial payment higher because of the increased costs of production.
Even in this connection a doubt has been raised in the minds of farmers. Within the

Canadian Wheat Board Act
last week I have received one or two letters, one in particular, suggesting that before we support this agreement we should secure a pledge from the government that every dollar in that fund will be distributed to the farmers in 1950. I have taken it upon myself to write back and say I am convinced that no government could withhold money which was properly due the producers of this country. That formed a part of the agreement, and is written into the statutes of this country.
I do not want, nor as you may well understand, Mr. Speaker, do my colleagues want to jeopardize this bill. Certainly we do not want to play into the hands of the people who, for economic reasons, are desirous of destroying this measure which is so important to western Canada. I have lived in the west long enough to recollect the struggle which has gone on since 1919 for the establishment of a wheat board. Election after election was fought in western Canada on that issue; in 1921, 1925, 1926, 1930 and even 1935. In each of those elections the wheat board method of marketing figured, and I am convinced that the people who sent us here want this legislation. They do not like some features of it. We do not like some features of it, but if the administration would indicate rather more clearly than they have the situation regarding the 1945 crop and, if possible, pay the participation certificates on that crop year, to a large extent they would satisfy the farmers.

If I may say a word, the position is that the 1943 payments are not quite out. The 1944 payments will start shortly, as the minister will indicate. It would be a physical impossibility to begin to make the 1945 payments earlier than late in 1948. The question is, how much advantage is to be gained; and when hon. members see the figure as to what the amount is, I think they will pretty well agree that is not an important factor.

When I hear the figure as to what the amount is, it may make a difference. I want it to be clearly understood that we are not opposing this measure, that indeed we are firmly in support of the principle of this bill. We are merely trying to emphasize the point of view we expressed when this legislation was in committee. We want, however, to see this system of orderly marketing not only carried into wheat but, as we said when this was being discussed, into coarse grains as well. When the bill following this one comes in, dealing with commodity marketing, we hope we may not only be able to give it our support but be able to suggest 83166-87
that it be strengthened and extended in scope and time as we would like to see it extended.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to speak again in this debate, but in view of some of the statements made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) I feel obliged to make a few comments.
The minister has suggested that if those who believe in the wheat board start pushing a measure of this kind around it may have a disastrous effect on the legislation. We appreciate that fact. But I assure the minister that we do not like being put in a position where we have to criticize a measure of this kind for this group has time and again made it perfectly clear that they believe in the principle of the wheat board taking delivery of all the wheat produced and also in the principle of a long-term international agreement on wheat. But just because we believe in that, we cannot be put in the position of having to remain silent when we consider that certain injustices are included in the bill. We dealt with those injustices when the bill was in committee.
There are three things to which the Minister of Agriculture referred. First of all, we believe that the year 1945 should be taken out of the pool altogether; second, we believe that the price of $1.35 should be raised to $1.55, and, third, we believe that the government should definitely commit itself to buy all the wheat produced within the pool period at the designated price, whether it be $1.35 or raised to $1.55. When discussing in committee whether it would be possible to invest these moneys in securities the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) said:
I do not know whether I should get into this controversy too deeply because no doubt this matter has been debated a great deal. The
principles of this contract are, I think, these: for the protection of floors throughout the later years of the contract, the part of the contract beyond the period we can foresee; for the protection of the United Kingdom government's agreement to have regard to the fact that in the early years of the contract less than world market prices were paid; in return for the protection of those two factors the farmer is accepting less in the earlier year or years of the contract than the world market price.
The Minister of Justice did not seem to know whether it would be possible to make a payment. Now the Minister of Agriculture says that he cannot possibly visualize a situation where a surplus would be allowed to accrue and remain unpaid. The Minister of Justice refused to state whether the payment would be made. He could not say that it

would be paid because the surplus might be required to meet losses in the latter part of the agreement.
Just what is likely to be the situation in the latter part of the agreement? The Minister of Justice states that there may be a very large crop and very low prices and that therefore the surplus may be required to meet the losses. But what is the price that we are to get in the latter stage of the agreement? The agreement calls for $1.25 and then for $1.
The Minister of Agriculture has stated it is unthinkable that the United Kingdom will not carry out her part of the bargain; that is to say, that when arriving at a price at that stage they will take into consideration the fact that we were willing to let the United Kingdom have our wheat in the earlier stage of the agreement at prices considerably below the market price. But we have no guarantee that the present government in the United Kingdom will be in power then. Public opinion in Great Britain is being aroused to such an extent against this agreement that it is very hard for us to say what might happen. I mention that because in the mail yesterday I received a pamphlet, as no doubt other hon. members did, from Britain. It shows the kind of propaganda which is being carried on there against this agreement, and it makes one wonder what the attitude of the British people will be two or three years from now on this wheat question. One of the people connected with this pamphlet is a prominent Canadian who has played a big part in the marketing of wheat from this country. First, I quote from the last part of the article to show the man to whom I am referring to. The article is headed "The Wheat Racket". It is published in the Liberator Council, a monthly publication. I quote from the end of the article:
We are fortunate in having as a member of the Liberator Council a gentleman whose name is widely known in the international grain trade of pre-war days. He has had 40 years' experience of that trade, and for a number of years was the official London representative of the Canadian wheat pools, when they were selling wheat at half the present inflated price. He writes that the world wheat situation is now on the easy side since the Canadian crop started moving freely in November, and says: "There is every possibility, with urgent needs satisfied, of a world glut in the late spring or early summer of 1947, when Australia and Argentine crops, moving in December, will be in free competition with the U.S.A.
I have quoted from the last of the article to show the individual connected with this organization.

I have not heard the name of the individual, but I venture to say

from the description that it is clear to whom the hon. gentleman points. I think it was the individual who proposed the floor prices that are now in this contract.
I have not the slightest idea who he is.
I have a pretty good idea.
I think the minister might do well to give us his name. I should like to know who it was.

The individual who suggested the floor prices in the agreement for the last two years was Mr. James Rank, one of the chief milling industry men in Britain. He bought all the wheat for the Conservative government there when they were in power and I think he is still buying wheat for the present government.
Was he the selling agent for the pools in this period?

He was the man who proposed the floors in the last two years. He is one of the outstanding supporters of the other party, not the party in power in Britain now7. But I do not think there is any danger of any government in Britain going back on a contract made by another British government.
It makes this article all the worse if that type of individual is connected with the organization that wrote this article.
He is not connected with this organization. He is buying wheat for the British government because he knows how to buy wheat.

I was hoping to hear that he was an irresponsible individual, but apparently he is not, and he is a member of this organization. I have quoted from the article to emphasize that if that type of propaganda is continued it will be very hard for any British government to pay us a high price for our wheat in the latter stage of the agreement if the world price should fall to sixty-five cents as it did in 1921. I quote further from this article "The Wheat Racket":
It is well worth considering a few comparative figures when trying to see through the fog of false and contradictory statements that arise on all sides.
Before the war the average cost of Canadian wheat, on rail, was 80 cents per bushel.
In the depression of the 1930's it fell to between 30 cents and 40 cents per bushel, on rail.
In September, 1939, a few days before the outbreak of w7ar, it was selling at 55J cents per bushel, including shipping to England.
Now this country has signed an agreement w-ith Canada to take approximately two-thirds of her wheat over a period of years, at the all-in

high price of $4.55 per bushel, with freight and insurance additional. It is estimated by experts, that after allowing for increased costs of production this figure will give the Canadian farmer the nice profit of over 50 per cent.
What is not generally known in this country, because it has not been publicized in the British press, is that in December, 1945, a conference of Canadian farmers was convened in Ottawa, at which Mr. Gardiner, Minister of Agriculture, stated that wheat acreages must be reduced, in order to maintain the artificially high prices. In other words, the Canadian government is guilty of perpetrating the scandal of planned scarcity of wheat-the old, old tale. To give actual figures, the wheat area for 4946 was fixed at 23,400,000 acres, as against an average of
25,600,000	acres, a purposeful reduction of ten per cent.
The whole article goes along in the same vein and I shall not read it all, but it continues later on:
Had the government told the people of this country the truth in December, 1945, that the Ottawa agricultural conference accepted a reduction of 1,200,000 acres in the Canadian wheat growing areas, in order to keep up high prices, and that bread in Great Britain would be rationed and impoverished as a consequence, there would have been such an outcry as would have sent the government hurtling to an inevitable ^crash, for even eighty per cent of its own M.P. s have been kept in purposeful ignorance of the real facts.
The minister must agree that if that kind of false propaganda-I can only call it absolutely false-is circulated throughout England and a new government comes into power, it may be very hard for any government to maintain a price considerably above the world market price when the people have been told that there was a deliberate curtailment of acreage in order to maintain the price above the market level.

Having heard the article read, may I say that in mentioning the name of the person who had suggested the idea of floor prices for the last two years under the wheat contract, my idea was to emphasize the fact that both those who support the present government and those who supported the last government were in on the discussions, first under the first government and then later under this government. They expressed agreement with the principles underlying this agreement, Having heard what was said by some individual, I would say that Rank was not the individual.

I should like to quote this again:
We are fortunate in having as a member of the liberator council a gentleman whose name is widely known in the international grain trade of pre-war days.
The liberator council there referred to is the organization that is circulating this pamphlet.
He has had forty years' experience of that trade, and for a number of years was the official London representative of the Canadian wheat pools.
It does not say that he wrote this article, but it says more or less that he is a member of the organization circulating the pamphlet.
That is a different gentleman.
Who are the people who signed it? Does it give any names?

There is Sir Charles
Morgan-Webb.
Who is he?
Probably the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) knows who he is.
It sounds like a fortuneteller.

I do not think the Minister of Labour had better betray his ignorance by making a statement of that kind. Then there is Mr. William Brown, Mr. G. H. Stock and Mr. Eric Troward. I think Sir Charles Morgan-Webb is fairly well known and it is absurd of the Minister of Labour to refer to him as a fortune-teller. I read that to point out the difficult position any government in England is bound to be in if that kind of propaganda is circulated now and the people of Britain told that they are having to pay us fifty per cent more than they should for our wheat when actually we are under-selling the world market by more than fifty per cent. How much more difficult will it be for us to obtain from Great Britain a price that is fifty per cent above the world market price, as may be the case in 1948 or 1949 should the world market price of wheat fall to seventy-five cents a bushel and we are to get $1.25. Then take into consideration the fact that we are taking less than the market price now. What will the reaction be at that time if this kind of propaganda is going on now when we are making a sacrifice of from seventy-five cents to ninety cents a bushel? The minister must realize the difficulty the government will be in.
In view of the fact that our farmers are making considerable sacrifice, the least thing the government can do is to guarantee to them that it will buy at the stipulated price all the wheat produced during the pool period. Surely it is not asking the government to go very far to do such a thing. The other day the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) accused me of not having faith

in the government in this matter, but I say that he is not being fair with the people. The Minister of Agriculture says to wait until 1950, and I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce suggested that we can wait until 1950 to decide this question, but the farmers are now being asked to go into an agreement and to make a sacrifice in the first part of that agreement, in return for which they are to get a certain guarantee during the latter part.
What right has the Minister of Trade and Commerce or the Minister of Agriculture to suggest that the farmers should have to wait until 1950 to know what they will get in return for making a sacrifice today? They should know that now. They should be told definitely that the government will take all wheat, not merely the wheat they will have room for. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) said that there might be a tremendous crop in 1949, with consequent low prices. If that is the situation, then in all probability the elevators will be plugged and the farmers will not be able to deliver their wheat. That is the time they will need a guarantee.
When you talk about faith I think the very least the government can do is to keep faith with the farmers and make that unconditional guarantee that it will take all the wheat produced during that period. The fact that the government refuses to give that understanding can only give the farmers the idea that it does not intend to keep faith with them.
On behalf of our group, I wish to say that we believe in the *wheat board. We want to support it. However we feel obliged to support the amendment to refer this bill back unless we have a definite guarantee from the government that it will buy all the wheat produced within that period of time.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to follow the various arguments that have been advanced here this afternoon and evening, but I do intend to try to return the mind of the house to the subject matter of the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken). The amendment is:
That the said bill be not now read the third time, but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole for the purpose of reconsidering sections 20, 21 and 22 thereof.
Those three sections deal with the questions of the pool period and the holding of surplus moneys secured or earned during the five-year period. As was explained by the leader of the opposition, the purpose of the amendment is to make provision by statute

and not by political promise for the payment of participation certificates for the crop year 1945-46. That is the purpose of this amendment which represents the demands of farmers all over western Canada. That is admitted by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) when he said that there was only the one point at issue, that, that they believe that the 1945 crop should not be put in the pool.
There have been many matters raised and smoke-screens produced; but, to come back to the amendment, let it be perfectly clear that reconsideration by the committee is for one purpose only, to assure the farmers and producers throughout this country that they shall in fact have carried out by the government the promise, whether made directly or not, certainly the contract promised that they should be entitled to secure whatever is earned on the 1945 crop. So far as this amendment is concerned, every hon. member who votes against it votes in favour of refusing to the farmers of this country, as soon as the necessary financial computations have been made, the right to participation certificates for the 1945 crop. There is the issue; there is no other. It is not a question of defeating any act; it is not a question of holding up any act. The smoke-screen that is raised is the usual one; it is that of always ascribing motives to those who are desirous of assuring that in this case the farmer shall receive what is his due instead of it being left to a nebulous promise which may or may not be carried out.
There is no denial by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) that the farmers demand this. There is no denial that, as recently as the end of February, in its submission to the government the federation of agriculture used these words:
We protest the action of the government in not retiring participation certificates on wheat delivered to the Canadian wheat board during the crop year 1945-48. We cannot but regard the withholding of these payments as contrary to the understanding which wheat growers had with the government during the whole of that crop year.
There is the essence of this motion, namely, to carry into effect what the federation of agriculture has asked for and what farmers everywhere are demanding. What is the government's attitude? We have not had any reply yet from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon). He is persistently silent when it comes to answering questions.

I will answer them pretty soon.

Canadian Wheat Board Act

At last he is being pried loose and will be answering questions asked the other day by the leader of the opposition and repeated today. How much is there to the credit of the 1944 and 1945 crop years? How much interest is paid in respect of the surpluses held? These are questions which were asked ten days ago. These are questions that as yet remain unanswered and would have remained unanswered but for the fact that today the leader of the opposition moved this amendment.
I ask my hon. friends to the left, did they not suggest this afternoon, and during the debate the payment of participation certificates on the 1945 crop? They are given the opportunity to vote in favour of what they contended for. What is the reply of the government? The government produces a bill which will become a statute and which will deny the payment of participation certificates during the five-year period, on the 1945 crop. This is one of these bills, sir, which when it becomes law, cannot be amended by order in council with the facility with which statutes were amended during the period of the War Measures Act and the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, because the other day the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) said that, so far as this bill is concerned, it does not derive its powers from the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act. That being so, no order in council can be made in 1948 which will make provision for payment of participation certificates on the 1945 crop.

The house will be
meeting.

The house is meeting now; and if the government intends to carry out the political promise, if I may call it that, which was made by the Minister of Agriculture, let us do it tonight so that the farmers will know what they are to get. I remember promises regarding the payment of participation certificates which were made before-
Not in 1939.
There were no participation certificates at any time under R.B. because the act did not come into effect until 1935.

The suggestion that by voting for this amendment you vote against the principle of the bill is entirely removed from the facts. The principle has been established. This is but one item; this is but one clause. Instead of postponing the matter for one or more years hence, I suggest that we complete this matter tonight.
I am glad that we are to get some information tonight from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) in reference to the amount of money on hand to the credit of the farmers, because up to the present, so far as the wheat board is concerned, it has shown a cavalier disregard of the rights of parliament. We have never been able to get any information. The attitude has been the attitude of the government under order in council denying the farmers of western Canada the right to an accounting of the moneys that rightfully belong to them.
I am not going to say any more on this occasion. I return to what I started with. This amendment is definite and to the point. It covers three paragraphs which have to do with the mechanics of operation, payment of participation certificates and the like, and it will give hon. members an opportunity of carrying out the wishes of Canadian agriculture and its representative, the federation of agriculture.

I purpose answering these questions and possibly adding slightly to some of the information, which will be of interest to hon. members, in connection with the funds on hand with the Canadian wheat board, the property of the producers of grain in western Canada.
The question was asked: What money is being held on hand today from the 1943 crop account? Before giving the answer, I should like to state that there is on hand today with the Canadian wheat board, from the 1940, 1941 and 1942 crop accounts, the sum of

$5,000,000. Let me point out whose property that money is. I may make this statement in connection with other crop years because for some members of this house it is quite unnecessary for me to make any explanation, though I believe there are members, who, hearing these figures quoted, may feel that these moneys have some relation to the funds for which distribution is asked for the 1945 crop.
As I say, from the 1940, 1941 and 1942 crop accounts there is on hand a total of $5,000,000. That is, producers' money is being paid out as the participation certificates are turned in and payments applied for. In this connection I may say that every effort is being made by the wheat board to get this money out into the hands of the rightful owners. Numerous letters have been written and follow-ups sent, and everything possible has been done to have the real owners of the money to apply for it and to have it paid.
From the 1943 crop account there is a balance of $6,000,000 on hand today, or there was a day or two ago. That money is also going out as it is being applied for by holders of participation certificates for the crop year of 1943. That money is, not wheat board money; it is the property of the grain producers.
From the 1944 crop account, subject to final accounting, although these are definite, authoritative figures, there is the sum of $61 million, again farmers' money on hand, distribution of which to the individual farmer will commence as early as possible this summer.
In the 1945 crop account, subject to final accounting, though the figures are relatively accurate, after allowing for the adjustment payment of ten cents a bushel which has been provided for by government policy this year, there is left on hand a total of $36 million. These are authoritative figures.
I was asked by the leader of the opposition for the investment return to the wheat board on securities that they hold representing investments of surplus producers funds. The leader of the opposition knows, as do the rest of us, that Mr. Strachey made another statement in Canada which has been referred to already in this house, and that was that it would be monstrous for anyone to question the good faith of any British government as regards living up to the letter of the agreement that they have made with the government of Canada.
