Withdraw the accusation you made before.

If, by referring this
matter back to a committee of the whole, it might have the effect of destroying this legislation, then those people, referring to the special interests here, would be very happy. That is what I wish to indicate.
There is no suggestion in this amendment that the bill would be destroyed by referring it back for the consideration of one item.

I have only another sentence or two. I want to impress upon this house and upon anyone interested in western agriculture that this legislation is necessary for the successful carrying out of the agreement with the United Kingdom. It is an attempt to give the grain producer stability of prices over a term of years. If anything should happen to defeat the legislation I believe the wheat producers of western Canada would wait some considerable time for another opportunity to obtain stability of prices.

I should like to say a few words before the

Canadian Wheat Board Act
vote is taken. I wish to assure the minister that there are at least some in this house who do not desire to have this legislation defeated. However, if it is defeated I should say it would be the fault of the government, because they have refused to make the very minor yet important changes that some of us in this house have desired. It is not the proper thing, I take it, for the government to endeavour to use the big stick on members of this house in order to force this legislation through, when I believe they could easily have it passed unanimously.
As the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) has said, we are agreeable to legislation of this type covering long-term payments to the farmers and stabilized prices. There is no question about that. We are also satisfied that the contract with Great Britain should be carried out. I may say quite frankly that we do not agree with some aspects of it, but in the main we are quite agreeable to seeing it fulfilled. However, as far as may be possible we are determined to have the government declare themselves on one thing. If they are as sincere as they try to make out they should not be so hesitant about saying they will pay the farmers the stipulated price for all wheat produced and offered for sale within the pool period. Certainly there can be no objection to that, and in that regard the government cannot hold any stick over my head and influence my vote. I tell them right now that if they do not agree to this I shall vote against them; that is, if they do not agree to take all the wheat produced within that pool period and pay the farmers the stipulated price.
If I may say just a sentence or two-
I wish you would clear that up, and you can take a dozen sentences.

While the bill was in committee, I took occasion to speak on behalf of the government on that very point. I can repeat now, and I wish to repeat, that the government anticipates there will be storage in western Canada to take every bushel of grain grown during this pool period. The government intends to take every bushel of grain grown and offered for sale by the farmers, to the extent of every available bushel of storage space. If I were able to go farther now I should like to do so, but you cannot project yourself into the future and know what the situation will be three years from now. It is not practical to say what we can do under certain circumstances that we do
not expect to exist. It is the intention of the government to take every bushel of wheat the farmers offer for sale during the pool period, and to distribute to the holders of participation certificates all the surplus money made during that period.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: la the first place, Mr. Speaker, I should like to observe that if the amendment were to carry and the bill were to go back to committee I am satisfied that, unless the government were ready to move an amendment along the lines suggested by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken), no such change could be made, because it might mean a charge upon the crown. So this amendment can be only one thing, a delaying or dilatory amendment, because it could not bring about the result he desires without the approval of the crown.
This is not the money of the government. Who said it was?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I submit that, on the face of it, the observation by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) was well justified; that this is a dilatory and delaying motion which clearly indicates where the official opposition stands on this important measure.
More imputing of motives.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
If you have a guilty conscience, of course attribute the motives to yourself.
In regard to the general principle of this bill I am one of those who are in thorough agreement with the idea that we should have a certain measure of stability over a reasonable period of years. I am one of those, too, who think five years is not too long. In fact, many of the farmers in my constituency feel they would like to be guaranteed a reasonable price and reasonable stability for more than five years at a time. If the principle is once written into the law that we should have a five-year pool and stability for five years it would be very hard, it seems to me, if it works out well, for any future government to depart from that principle. In other words, in this agreement and bill we have established the principle of a period of stability for five years at a time.
The attitude of hon. members opposite is this. They are attributing to themselves a :great deal of friendship for the farmer because they say: We would like to cut down this period from five to four years in order that there may be distributed at once, or when it [DOT]can be distributed, probably within the next three years, the sum of $36 million. I think myself that when this whole situation comes to be reviewed in the years ahead the friends of the farmers will say that it was well to leave that less than ten cents a bushel with dhe wheat board for perhaps an extra two

years for the sake of having a five-year period of stability established instead of a four-year period. In other words, we say that we want to have a five-year wheat pool period established as a minimum, and we say that, even if this money be paid out perhaps two years later than it otherwise would be paid out, that is a small price to pay for establishing the principle of stability for a period of five years at a time.
The hon. member said, two years later. If it will take two years to make the 1945 payment it will be 1952 before we make the 1950 payment. Get your mathematics straight.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I did not think I would have to go into such details as that with my able friend the hon. member for Calgary West. We are perhaps three years behind now in making payments on a yearly basis. If it is all put in a five-year pool, presumably, instead of the money being paid out one year at a time and having five years to look after separately, it will be paid out at once, and it will not take nearly as long to pay it out in one payment as it would in five.
In regard to these attacks on the ground of delay in payments, I point out to the members of this house through you, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, in their submission to the government, unreservedly endorse the present wheat board and its present personnel. If they had thought that the wheat board was not doing a good job I submit that they would not have endorsed the present personnel of the board. I think that is clear.
So what?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: "So what," my hon. friend says. The suggestion is made that the wheat board is not doing a good job, that it is pushing the farmer around.
Who said so?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) accused the board of being bureaucrats.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: All I go by is this. I took part in the Portage la Prairie by-election and I saw the attacks made by the official opposition on this wheat agreement.
Made by whom?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: By the official opposition.
Name them.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Well, yourself.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is making a misstatement of fact. I never once criticized the wheat board in that by-election. I criticized the agreement and said it was wrong.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: That is what I said. That just shows again the desire of the official opposition to find fault. I said that the hon. member criticized the wheat agreement.
You said the board.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: After all, if we cannot agree on a simple matter like that it will be hard for us to agree on some of these other matters. I do say this. I took part in the Portage la Prairie by-election. It is all very well for the leader of the opposition and members to come into this house and say that they are in favour of the principle of the agreement and then proceed to find fault with it in every conceivable manner in order to break down confidence in the agreement throughout the country. They are trying to have it both ways, and when that is suggested to them and they get up and protest, it shows nothing more or less than a guilty conscience. They cannot have it both ways. They cannot go into a by-election like Portage la Prairie and attack this agreement as not being a good one and say that the arrangements made are not good, and then come into this house and pretend that they are in favour of the agreement.
We did not do that at all. We said that it was a bad agreement.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: There we have it. Are you speaking for your leader? I understood him to say that it was a good agreement?
No, he did not.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Let him deny it. I do not think the esteemed leader of the opposition needs the young man from Kamloops to speak for him. He has been long enough in public life to speak for himself and I do not think he would wish my hon. friend to speak for him.
I think I should pay a passing reference to my friends of the C.C.F. party. I am not unmindful of the fact that they brought the minister of agriculture of Saskatchewan into that Portage la Prairie by-election, and the Hon. Mr. Nollet in that by-election said that a child could have made a better agreement than this one, and asked the people to vote against the government candidate because the government had made such a poor agreement. There is the situation, and I say again to my friends of the C.C.F., let them say the same
thing in the house as they say out in the west. Let them not talk one way out there and another way in the house.

Mr. Speaker, I think the house should know that I had the honour of sharing a platform with the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) in the city hall at Regina before the present session opened. I would ask him whether I was there and whether I did not tell the truth about that agreement.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: You were charming as usual.
Mr. Speaker, I asked for a statement of truth, not an evasion like that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It is very hard for me to admit that the C.C.F. are fair-minded in everything they say because I cannot admit that they are.

Mr. Speaker, the charge has been made by the member for Rosthern that we have one story in the west and another story in the house. I had the pleasure of appearing on the same platform with the hon, member for Rosthern and I ask him, did I or did I not quote the terms of the agreement?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: In reply to the question asked me by the charming lady member for Qu'Appelle I would say this. On that occasion, as I heard her speech, I found no fault with what she said. In what I suggested I was particularly referring to Mr. Nollet, minister of agriculture of Saskatchewan, whom the C.C.F. brought in to take part in that federal by-election. I was not referring to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle.
Did the hon. member hear Mr. Nollet make the statement he has quoted?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It was reported in the newspapers and not denied.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must remind the house that we are not in committee. Is the house ready for the question?

The hon. member for Rosthern has imputed something to the movement which I have the honour to lead in this house, and I wish to tell him that no group in this house has been so consistent in support of the wheat agreement, both in and out of the house, as the C.C.F. group.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say to the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) in connection with what he has said: if he felt that Mr. Nollet, Minister of Agriculture in the Saskatchewan
Canadian Wheat Board Act

government, had ever said anything outside the legislature that he would not say inside the legislature, he had an opportunity to become a member of that legislature and to make his charges in that house when Mr. Nollet could have defended himself.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to take part in this debate, because on more than one occasion since the question has been before the house I have spoken not only for myself but on behalf of this group. But when the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) rises in his place in his usual blustering bull-dozing way and makes statements such as he has just made, I want to remind him of what he has been reminded of by the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bentley), namely, that he has not seen fit to accept the offer which was honestly and truly made by the C.C.F. in Saskatchewan.
I also want to tell him that I had an invitation to speak in the Rosthern constituency after the close of the last session. I appeared on a number of platforms there and I defended the wheat agreement to the constituents of Rosthern. I told them that no doubt their member was so busy chasing around other parts of the province that he would not have an opportunity to get into all parts of his own constituency before returning to Ottawa and that I was defending the wheat agreement on his behalf and on behalf of all those who believed in it. When the hon. member for Rosthern gets up on the floor of the house and for his own purposes, not for the sake of helping to put this bill through, makes the statements and assertions that he has made, I do not think he is doing himself or his party any good.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I ask the hon. member to withdraw. The hon. member has suggested that I did not get up in this debate to make a point, that I got up for my own purposes. I suggest that that is imputing motives. After all, if that is the way he feels about it, I will say to him that if the wheat agreement did not get a better defence than it has received from most C.C.F'ers out west who found fault with almost everything in it and then say that they are in favour of it-

The hon. member
knows better than that.
Question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Doubtless
there has been considerable heat during this argument and I suggest that some of the statements made have almost been un-

parliamentary. May I ask hon. members to restrain themselves as much as possible and endeavour to discuss the bill which is now before the house for third reading.

Mr. Speaker, I shall
endeavour to comply with your request as long as you keep certain members on the other side in order. When the hon. member for Rosthern gets pinned down to certain incidents, he shifts over to another scene and another part of Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member has
no right to say that. That is entirely out of order.

What is the point of
order? Eventually I shall have an opportunity to deal with the question before the house.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Why don't you?

Because there are so many foolish statements being made and, if a person does not answer them, they will go out unchallenged.
I just wanted to make one observation before getting down to business which is far too important to the farmers of this country to have side-tracked by some people trying to make a little political capital for themselves. There is no group in the political field in Saskatchewan that has been as consistent and persistent in working for the interests of the farmers as has the group to which I have the honour and privilege to belong.
Time.

I hope the ones who want to call "time" will not call too soon. When we were discussing the various stages of this bill we tried to impress upon the government the necessity of doing certain things in order to provide legislation that would give the farmers the benefits to which they are entitled. As has been mentioned on more than one occasion, the farmers of western Canada believe-so far there has been no satisfactory answer to the contrary-that there was no justification for taking the 1945 crop and placing it in the pool period. There are many farmers who have taken the attitude that the government, by doing that, has violated the agreement. When those farmers started to deliver grain from the 1945 crop it was understood that the wheat board was operating and would continue to operate on its previous basis, namely, a one-year pool. Later on, that crop year was incorporated in the five-year pool, and consequently many farmers believe that, although there may not

Canadian Wheat Board Act
have been a written undertaking between them and the government, the government has violated the spirit of the agreement between them.	.
I suggest to the government that there is a way out by which they can continue to carry out the greater portion of the plan they have in mind and satisfy the farmers that they are prepared to do the right thing. They should adopt the suggestions that we have made on a number of occasions when this question was before the house; that is, make provision to pay interim payments during the pool period at the end of the crop year and make those interim payments on the basis of providing parity to the farmers. I left my notes on the other desk so that I cannot state exactly how many millions of dollars the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) told the house was in the hands of the government being held on behalf of the farmers. I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce why it should take the government so much longer to distribute money due to the farmers than it used to take the pools when they were operating on the pooling basis. I thank him for the answer he gave, but it is not as complete as I should like to have. I hope that the government will be able to make a better working arrangement.
However the suggestion I wish to make to the government is that in making these interim payments they take the money out of the fund which belongs to the farmers. Make the interim payment to bring the payment for that year up to parity. If that is done you will be using only the farmers' money. There will still be a considerable amount of money left over which will be used in the pool and which you will distribute at the end of the pool period. I make that suggestion because I believe it can be done. I believe it is possible to do it. If that is done it will solve the problem in so far as the farmers are concerned. It is because they are keenly concerned that I am taking up the time of the house to make this one final plea. Let the government cooperate with us and we shall be prepared to cooperate in helping to do something for the farmers.

I do not intend to look around to find this blustering bulldozer because I have examined all the seats on the other side and I do not find anyone who would be in that frame of mind. In my opinion they all have their tails down and are
hunting a little shelter. They are not the kind of person that was described a moment ago.
What I wish to make plain, if I can, to those of us who sit on this side of the house and with a pious hope perhaps that what I am saying may penetrate the conscience of one or two over there-that is the most that I can expect-
Presumptuous.

I am very happy to know that. I thought I had missed something. Now that I have learned where the remark came from, compared with the minister, I am presumptuous. His modesty is something that we all know about.
What does this amendment seek to do? It asks that the proceeds of that crop shall be distributed. That is all. There is nothing else in it. When we are accused of acting for the Winnipeg grain exchange and trying to destroy what the government is doing, may I say that I think this is a more apt comparison. Let us assume that in his younger days the minister, who is in charge of this bill, went wooing a young and beautiful woman, and he had secured a beautiful corsage of roses. We all know that roses have thorns in them, but when we give a corsage to a woman whom we are trying to influence in our favour we have the thorns clipped off. What the government are doing here is saying to the farmers of the country, here is a bill. Certain features of it are good for you but you are going to take it with the thorns in it and like it. That is exactly what the government are doing at the present time by the refusal to distribute the proceeds of the 1945 crop.

In view of the representation made from this side of the house when the bill was before the committee, the government might be well advised to take into consideration the representations made. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) has intimated that there is a matter of $36 million involved which belongs to the producers of wheat.
It is not unreasonable to ask the administration to consider the matter overnight and bring in a recommendation along the lines which have been suggested. I cannot see that it would require any appropriation of government funds to carry out the terms of the suggestion. So far as the members of this group are concerned, if the government reconsiders the matter and refuses to make any compromise whatever we shall support the
Canadian Wheat Board Act

government on the third reading. I think the matter might be considered by the government overnight and a decision given tomorrow.
I was paired with the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth). Had I voted, I would have voted against the amendment.
I was paired with the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Dionne). Had I voted, I would have voted for the amendment.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT- COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS

speechtext: Right Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) moved the second reading of Bill No. 25, to provide for the sale and export of agricultural products.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT- COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext: Does the minister propose to make a statement at this stage?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT- COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext:
I made quite an
extended statement on the resolution, and I do not consider it necessary to make a similar statement at this time. However, I do want to make available to the opposition an amendment I hope to have moved when we are in committee, and I think the information should be given at this time, while wre are on second reading.
Some questions bearing on the marketing of apples were asked me on the resolution. I stated at that time that there had been discussions between the provincial apple board and representatives of the British government, as well as between the special products board and the British government, and that the members of the apple board were anxious to be put in a position where they could, during at least the transitional period, have an agreement with Britain for the marketing of apples. I also stated that it was not our intention at the moment to enter into other agreements except the apple agreement under the powers which are being asked for. I was asked definitely whether there was provision in the bill which made it possible for such an agreement to be entered into. I looked into that question carefully between then and now and, after submitting it to the officials of the Department of Justice, I was satisfied that there was no provision in the bill which made it certain that an agreement of that kind could be entered into. So I intend, when we are in committee, to move an amendment to section 5 which, I am assured, will make it possible for that agreement to be entered into. I should like to make copies of this amendment available to the leaders of the different parties tonight in order that they may be able to give it consideration.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT- COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext:
May I ask if the minister proposes to put forward any amendments to take care of that other portion of the request, namely, that the existing board should be permitted to carry on with interprovincial trade?
Bill read the third time and passed.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT- COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext:
That is the intention.
Privilege-Mr. Bracken

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT- COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext: Does this cover both export and interprovincial trade?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT- COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext: Yes, both.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT- COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under these circumstances I wonder whether it would not be a reasonable request that I should be permitted to adjourn the debate. There has been made at the time of second reading an important suggestion which will have a direct bearing on the debate that will ensue on the motion for second reading.
On motion of Mr. Stirling the debate was adjourned.
